content: 05 October, 2026 | Monday BioPharma America BioPharma Europe BioPharma Middle East BioPharma Africa BioPharma APAC Events Media Pack Login BioPharma Pharma & Biopharma Manufacturing Pharma Research Pharma QC Clinical Trials Drug Discovery Drug Approval BioSimilar Pharma Packaging LAB LAB Business LAB Health & Safety LAB Products LAB Design LAB Testing LifeScience Biotech Biologics BioSimilar Clinical & Diagnostic Emerging Biotech Vaccines BioChemicals Cell & Gene Antibody Drug Conjugates Contract Services Contract Research Clinical Research Contract Manufacturing Methods Development Pre-Clinical Outsourcing Bio Digital Digital Health Digital CRO’s Health CIO Digital Innovation Artificial Intelligence Patent Medtech Med’s Industry Medical Devices Medical Diagnostic Bio Marketing Bio Jobs Bio Special WhitePaper Product in Action Premium Article BioInvest Bio Informatics Webinar MasterControl Resource Centre Special Report Sustainable Biopharma Mergers and Acquisitions Bio Insight Bio Analysis Bio Feature Bio Reports Bio-Interaction BioResources Consumer Health Healthcare FemHealth Focus Endocrinology Neurology Cancer / Immunology Cancer / Oncology COVID19 Mental Health Diabetes Nutraceutical & Supplement Medicine Longevity Countries Australia New Zealand South Korea Japan Malaysia Thailand Singapore Indonesia India China Taiwan Hong Kong Vietnam SAARC Countries SEA Countries EMEA (Middle East & Africa) North America Europe World LifeScience Vaccines Moderna’s XFG-Targeting COVID-19 Vaccine Secures Singapore HSA Authorisation Moderna’s XFG-Targeting COVID-19 Vaccine Secures Singapore HSA Authorisation 29 September 2026 | Tuesday | News Spikevax XFG becomes Singapore’s first authorised COVID-19 vaccine targeting the JN.1-lineage XFG variant, with approval covering individuals aged six months and older. Moderna Singapore announced that the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) has approved/authorised Spikevax® XFG, Moderna’s updated COVID-19 mRNA vaccine targeting the SARS-CoV-2 XFG variant, for active immunisation against COVID-19 caused by SARS-CoV-2 in Singapore. Spikevax XFG is the first COVID-19 vaccine targeting the JN.1-lineage XFG variant to be authorised by HSA for use in Singapore as of 18 August 2026. The updated vaccine is designed to target XFG, a JN.1-lineage variant of SARS-CoV-2 that has been predominant globally [1] in recent months. It uses mRNA technology to give the body’s cells instructions to make the virus’s spike protein, helping the immune system recognise it and build an immune response. The authorisation comes as global public health, and regulatory authorities continue to review and update COVID-19 vaccine formulations as the virus evolves. For 2026–2027, European and U.S. regulators have identified XFG as the preferred JN.1-lineage variant for updated vaccines, while World Health Organization (WHO) has said that XFG-targeting vaccine formulations may be used when supported by evidence of a strong immune response against COVID-19 variants that are currently circulating. “HSA authorisation of Spikevax XFG reflects the importance of continuing to evolve our approach to COVID-19 prevention as the virus changes over time,” said Evelyn Pang, General Manager of Moderna Singapore. “The availability of an updated vaccine targeting the XFG variant provides healthcare professionals and patients with an additional option as part of ongoing efforts to protect those at increased risk of severe COVID-19.” “COVID-19 does not need to be making headlines for prevention to matter,” said Dr Leong Hoe Nam, Medical Director, Rophi Clinic and Senior Consultant Infectious Diseases Physician. “For older adults, individuals with weakened immune systems and those living with chronic conditions, COVID-19 repeatedly causes serious illness and upends everyday life. Endemic means a persistent daily threat and not harmlessness. Staying up to date with vaccination is a practical and crucial way to help reduce this threat for those at risk, in line with national recommendations.” “As Singapore's population ages, prevention has an increasingly important role in helping people stay healthy, independent and active,” said Dr Leong Choon Kit, Family Medicine Specialist, Mission (Hougang) Medical Clinic, and co-author of Singapore’s Adult Vaccination Guidelines. “For many people, especially older and those with chronic conditions, a timely conversation with a doctor can help ensure preventive care is considered alongside their broader health needs. An updated COVID-19 vaccines gives healthcare professionals another option when discussing prevention with patients, taking into account their age, health conditions and individual circumstances.” "Many people are surprised to learn that influenza and COVID-19 vaccines can be given during the same visit, where clinically appropriate," said Dr Aziz Noordin, Family Physician and Director, Tampines Family Medicine Clinic, and Chairperson of GP+ Co-operative. "They are caused by different viruses, but both can cause serious illness in older adults and people with chronic medical conditions. Discussing both vaccines during one visit can be a simple, practical way to stay up to date with recommended vaccinations, with advice tailored to individual health needs." In Singapore, COVID-19 vaccination continues to be recommended for people at increased risk of severe illness, including those aged 60 and above, medically vulnerable individuals aged six months and above, and residents of aged-care facilities. Healthcare workers and those living or working with medically vulnerable individuals are also encouraged to consider vaccination, while others aged six months and above may choose to receive it. Spikevax XFG is approved in Singapore as a multidose vial presentation for individuals aged six months and older and as a pre-filled syringe presentation for individuals aged 12 years and older. Author(s)Sabrina McCrear, Jeffery A. Goad, PharmD, MPH Fact checked by: Maggie L. Shaw Without a functioning ACIP, Jeffery Goad, PharmD, MPH, explains who now guides COVID-19 vaccine use and how HMOs can stock vaccines. Advertisement Captions are auto-generated. In May 2026, the FDA’s Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (VRBPAC) recommended that COVID-19 vaccines for the 2026-2027 season target the JN.1-lineage XFG variant.1 The decision aligned with trends documenting seasonal upticks in COVID-19 cases, as reports of the BA.3.2 variant, commonly known as Cicada, increased in the spring and XFG, known as Stratus, later became the most common variant detected in Bay Area wastewater.2,3 Yet the current recommendation process for COVID-19 vaccines was missing a key recommendation from the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), Jeffery A. Goad, PharmD, MPH, professor of pharmacy practice at Chapman University School of Pharmacy, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® (AJMC®). VRBPAC typically recommends COVID-19 vaccines first, then ACIP. Unlike influenza vaccines, which have a perpetual recommendation, COVID-19 vaccines technically need a CDC recommendation each season, Goad explained. Without what he described as a functioning ACIP, VRBPAC’s recommendation stands without support from the CDC. “In lieu of that, what we have are associations such as the American Academy of Family Physicians and the American Academy of Pediatrics, who are making the recommendations now that providers should follow for the use of COVID-19 vaccines this season,” he explained. Goad noted that ACIP also generally publishes a yearly Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) with its influenza recommendations, although influenza vaccines do not technically need it from the FDA’s standpoint. Goad also addressed vaccine stocking concerns for health maintenance organizations (HMOs) amid the recommendation uncertainty. He said all 4 available COVID-19 vaccines are “equally about as effective,” though they differ in their age indications. He did note, however, that HMOs with a wide variety of patients may need to use Moderna’s Spikevax, which is approved for children as young as 6 months. Spikevax is approved for all adults 65 and older and for those 6 months through 64 years with at least 1 underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe COVID-19.4 For mostly adult patient populations, “you could use any of the vaccines and stock any of them.” References 1. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, October 4, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Pirbright Study Links COVID-19 Immunity to Bat Coronavirus Protection by Bioengineer October 2, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Scientists at The Pirbright Institute and King’s College London have revealed that immunity generated by SARS-CoV-2 infection or vaccination may offer significant protection against a range of other bat coronaviruses. This discovery, published in two companion articles in PLOS Biology, suggests that the widespread exposure of the human population to SARS-CoV-2 has inadvertently raised the biological barrier for related viruses attempting to spill over from animal reservoirs. The research provides a critical new perspective on pandemic preparedness, indicating that the immune landscape shaped by the current pandemic could serve as a partial shield against future zoonotic threats from the sarbecovirus sub-group. The study focused on sarbecoviruses, the specific sub-group of coronaviruses that includes both SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2. Researchers examined how these viruses interact with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2, or ACE2, the cellular receptor that many coronaviruses utilize to enter host cells. By investigating the ability of various bat coronaviruses to use ACE2 proteins from a broad spectrum of species, the team aimed to understand the host range of these viruses. This host range is a key determinant of spillover risk, as viruses capable of infecting a wide variety of animals are generally considered more likely to jump to humans. The team analyzed fifteen representative bat coronavirus spike proteins using libraries of ACE2 receptors derived from thirty-four different species. These species included humans, livestock, rodents, and animals previously proposed as intermediate hosts in the transmission chain. The analysis revealed a distinct pattern in receptor usage among the different evolutionary groups of bat sarbecoviruses. Specifically, the researchers identified so-called generalist sarbecoviruses, which can utilize ACE2 receptors from many different species, and found that these were largely confined to the same evolutionary lineage as SARS-CoV-2. Discover more Veterinarians Health News infecting Scientific Institutions Infectious Diseases Dr. Nazia Thakur, a postdoctoral scientist at Pirbright and the lead author of the study, explained that the bat coronaviruses currently considered most likely to spill over into humans are also the most likely to be recognized by existing COVID-19 immunity. She noted that while the risk of spillover can never be entirely eliminated, the global exposure to SARS-CoV-2 may have created a more robust immune defense against related viruses. This finding implies that the immune systems of many people are already primed to recognize and neutralize potential future pathogens that share structural similarities with the virus that caused the current pandemic. The research also highlighted the dynamic nature of viral evolution during the pandemic. The team investigated how the host range of SARS-CoV-2 itself has changed over time. They found that variants, particularly those within the Omicron lineage, acquired specific mutations in the receptor binding domain. These mutations resulted in shifting patterns of ACE2 usage across different animal species, demonstrating that the relationship between viral evolution and host susceptibility is not static but continuously evolving in response to immune pressure and environmental factors. To assess the practical implications for human health, the scientists examined blood samples from individuals who had recovered from COVID-19. The antibodies present in these samples were tested against a range of bat coronaviruses to measure their neutralizing capacity. The results showed that these antibodies successfully neutralized a variety of closely related bat coronaviruses. This cross-neutralization indicates that the immune response triggered by SARS-CoV-2 is not strictly specific to that single virus but extends to a broader family of related pathogens, providing a layer of protection against potential new infections. Professor Katie Doores of King’s College London emphasized that the viruses showing the strongest antigenic similarity to SARS-CoV-2 were the most readily recognized and neutralized by the antibodies generated following infection. In contrast, more distantly related bat coronaviruses tended to be specialists, capable of using ACE2 receptors from only a limited range of hosts. However, the researchers also detected lower levels of neutralization against these more distant viruses, suggesting that there is some degree of broader protection even against pathogens that are not closely related to SARS-CoV-2. Discover more infections Biological Sciences CoV-2 Medical Literature & Resources COVID-19 Further experiments conducted at both institutions identified several monoclonal antibodies capable of recognizing a remarkably diverse range of sarbecoviruses. The second companion article in the study detailed where these monoclonal antibodies bind on the viral surface, highlighting conserved regions of the coronavirus spike protein. These conserved regions are less likely to mutate without compromising the virus’s ability to infect cells, making them ideal targets for the development of next-generation vaccines and therapeutics. This approach could lead to the creation of pan-sarbecovirus vaccines that offer protection against multiple strains simultaneously. Dr. Dalan Bailey, head of the Viral Glycoproteins group at Pirbright, described the evidence of cross-neutralization of even some distantly related bat coronaviruses as an encouraging finding. He suggested that this capability points toward the feasibility of developing broadly protective vaccines or therapeutics that can cover a wide spectrum of sarbecoviruses. By targeting conserved epitopes, such interventions could provide a more durable and comprehensive defense against future zoonotic spillover events, reducing the likelihood of a new pandemic emerging from the bat reservoir. The work underscores the importance of understanding virus host range, receptor usage, and immune recognition in an integrated manner rather than in isolation. By identifying the specific characteristics that distinguish higher-risk viruses from those less likely to spill over into humans, researchers hope to strengthen global pandemic preparedness efforts. This study provides a scientific basis for monitoring specific bat coronavirus lineages and developing targeted interventions that leverage existing immunity to protect against future viral threats, ultimately contributing to a more resilient global health system. Respiratory illnesses increasing as fall approaches in California KCRA / KQCA US LIVE Current Time 0:00 / Total Duration 0:57 Sorry, this video is not available, please check back later. Advertisement Updated: 7:28 AM PDT Sep 29, 2026 Editorial Standards i Julian Gaskins Producer Daniel Macht Digital Media Manager COVID-19 and other respiratory illnesses increase as fall approaches in California Updated: 7:28 AM PDT Sep 29, 2026 Editorial Standards i Julian Gaskins Producer Daniel Macht Digital Media Manager As fall approaches, respiratory illnesses are beginning to rise in California, with health officials noting increases in strep throat, common colds, and COVID-19 cases. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported that strep throat infections are increasing as children return to school. Common cold viruses are also on the rise, and while flu and RSV activity remain low nationwide, they are expected to increase in the coming weeks. Advertisement California is also seeing a significant rise in COVID-19 cases. "It's a late-summer surge, later than last year, but this is the highest number of COVID cases that we've seen since last summer's surge, so the activity level right now is very high," said Dr. Dean Blumberg of UC Davis Health Pediatric Infectious Diseases. Blumberg said that in California the highest surges for the past two years have been in the summer, and he wasn't quite sure why. "In general, the first time you get COVID should be the worst," Blumberg said of symptoms. But a big exposure to the virus could make for a more severe illness. Overall, rates of the illness are "less severe" at this "waning end of the pandemic," he said. Earlier in the pandemic, COVID had a higher risk of hospitalization and death than influenza, but that has since flipped, Blumberg said. For those who are interested in antiviral treatment with Paxlovid, Blumberg recommended getting tested. "The earlier it's done, the more effective it is," he said, adding that people should go to an urgent care to get a prescription for antivirals if it might take their regular provider longer to get back to them. Paxlovid stops the virus from multiplying and "works best" for those at the highest risk of severe illness: people who are age 65 or older, immunocompromised or who are most at severe risk of complications. COVID-19 and flu vaccines are now available and recommended for everyone over the age of 6 months. RSV vaccinations are also available for infants, older adults, and pregnant women, who can receive the shot in late pregnancy. Blumberg said that antivirals for influenza shorten the duration of the illness. content_title: Respiratory virus season has arrived. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV vaccines this fall
content: Respiratory virus season has arrived. Here’s what to know about flu, Covid-19 and RSV vaccines this fall There’s a bit of a chill in the air, pumpkin spice in your coffee and children back to school — which means the threat of respiratory viruses like Covid-19, influenza and RSV is looming. Some respiratory illnesses have arrived already. Seasonal influenza activity is still low at the national level, data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows. But certain flu metrics are inching up – especially in the West . Health officials in Washington state’s King County note that since mid-August there has been an increase in people with flu visiting emergency departments in the area. Related video above | When is the best time to get your flu shot? Vaccines that help prevent illness and reduce the risk of serious infections and hospitalization are now available, and for some people, this is the right time to roll up their sleeves. Typically, the CDC launches a fall campaign around this time of year, recommending seasonal immunizations such as the flu shot and Covid-19 vaccines. But after sweeping changes to the agency’s vaccine advisory committee during the second Trump administration and ongoing lawsuits, the CDC recently posted guidance online to follow last year’s recommendations for flu and Covid-19. Meanwhile, the American Medical Association and the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project launched their own independent reviews of this fall’s vaccines – including those for flu , Covid and RSV – which were published in September in the medical journal JAMA. The review papers helped inform 2026-27 respiratory virus immunization recommendations released by several medical groups, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “For more than 60 years, the United States has benefited from an established federal process for evaluating vaccine evidence and translating that science into recommendations for the American public. At the center of that process were the Centers for Disease Control and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the ACIP,” Dr. Bruce Gellin, board chair of the Vaccine Integrity Project and professor of medicine at Georgetown University, said at a news briefing. “Unfortunately today, the federal government is not fulfilling that responsibility in the way that it historically has. But the need for that work has not disappeared. Influenza, SARS-CoV-2 and the RSV viruses will circulate again this fall and winter,” Gellin said. “Clinicians will still have patients to care for. Parents will still have decisions to make for their children, and older Americans, pregnant women and people with underlying health conditions will still need to know how best to protect themselves,” he said. “We cannot allow the breakdown of a federal process to create a vacuum in evidence-based vaccine guidance.” The US Department of Health and Human Services has not responded to CNN’s request for comment on the groups’ recommendations. Flu, Covid-19 and RSV immunizations are now available at most major pharmacies. “And really reassuringly, insurers have indicated to the major groups that they will cover these respiratory virus immunizations,” Dr. Sarah Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians, said in a news briefing. Ordering through Vaccines for Children, the federal program that provides routine immunizations at no cost to children who are uninsured or underinsured or whose families may not otherwise be able to afford them, has also started. About half of US children are eligible for the program. “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories. They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives,” Nosal said in a news release. “As federal guidance evolves, the science behind vaccines remains strong. These recommendations are grounded in the latest evidence, informed by public health experts and shaped by what family physicians are seeing every day in their patients.” RSV immunization Who should get it The groups eligible for RSV immunizations include older adults, pregnant people and infants. “People age 50 and older with high-risk conditions, and everyone over 75 years old, should get one dose,” Nosal said. “This is not an annual vaccine. If you got one before, you do not need a new one this year. Getting one should protect you throughout the entire season.” During pregnancy, RSV vaccination is recommended in the third trimester, between weeks 32 and 36. Children younger than 8 months should be immunized against RSV using a monoclonal antibody unless their mother got an RSV vaccination during pregnancy, said Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “If the mother’s immunization status is unknown, that child should be immunized,” Racine said in the briefing. He added that children between 8 months and 19 months of age who are in certain high-risk groups for severe disease are also recommended to get the RSV monoclonal antibody. And a single dose of RSV vaccine is recommended for adults who have weakened immune systems. “Immunosuppressed individuals are at higher risk for severe disease than immunocompetent individuals,” Dr. Dan Barouch, director of the Center for Virology and Vaccine Research at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, who was not involved in the new recommendations, said in an email. “The vaccines are also generally less effective in immunosuppressed individuals compared with immunocompetent individuals.” When to get it For older adults, RSV vaccinations are typically recommended in late summer and early fall. The advice slightly changed this year for pregnant people. “ACOG now recommends that pregnant individuals receive a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine, Abrysvo, from September 1 through March 1 instead of only through January 31,” Dr. Christina Davidson, chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, said in the news briefing. “We made this change because the RSV disease season is now occurring later in the spring, and it is also more severe than it used to be,” Davidson said. “The extension of the eligibility window will help provide pregnant patients and their infants with additional protection.” For infants, the RSV monoclonal antibody is typically recommended around virus season, from October through March. Seasonal flu shots Who should get it Everyone 6 months and older is recommended to get an annual flu shot. “On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to go to the doctor by 30% to 60%,” Nosal said. “Adults 65 years and older should get an enhanced flu vaccine, one that is high-dose, adjuvanted or recombinant, when it’s available,” she said. “But do not delay your vaccination if that one’s not available.” And for the first time, an mRNA-based flu vaccine is available for use in adults 50 and older. The flu vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy, but pregnant people should avoid the nasal spray version, according to the recommendations. “Pregnant and postpartum people still have a significantly higher risk of developing serious complications from infection compared with non-pregnant people,” Davidson said. “The inactivated or recombinant influenza vaccines remain the only vaccines that are recommended for use in pregnancy in any trimester, so please work with your OB care clinician or pharmacist to get these,” she said. “Most importantly, if you are able to get the vaccine while you are pregnant, the immunity will also, in part, pass on to your baby.” When to get it October is the ideal time to get vaccinated, Nolan said, because “protection wanes throughout the season.” Some providers use the slogan “ flu before boo ” to remind people to get a flu shot before Halloween. Updated Covid-19 vaccines Who should get it Getting an updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for adults. “If you’re older than 19, we recommend getting the Covid-19 vaccine,” Nosal said. “This is especially important for people who are 65 years and older, at increased risk for severe Covid infection and those who’ve never received a Covid-19 vaccine,” she said. “For those adults 65 years and older, they should receive a second dose of the updated Covid-19 vaccine six months after that season’s initial dose to help maintain protection as immunity wanes over time.” The vaccine is also recommended for infants between 6 months and 23 months of age, and children in certain high-risk groups or those whose families request vaccination. And for people who are immunocompromised, the annual updated Covid-19 vaccine is recommended for ages 6 months and older. Last year, the CDC recommended Covid-19 vaccines based on conversations with the patient’s healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making, Barouch noted, but the agency “also emphasized that the risk-benefit of the vaccines is most favorable for individuals who are at higher risk of severe disease.” Davidson, of ACOG, said the vaccine is also recommended during pregnancy. “The most important message is this: If you are pregnant, considering pregnancy or are a new or breastfeeding parent, please get your vaccine or your annual booster. All four of the available Covid vaccines are safe for you,” Davidson said. Moderna offers two mRNA shots, Pfizer and BioNTech have another, and Sanofi and Novavax offer a more traditional protein-based version. “A recommendation for the Covid vaccine is based on more than five years of research and millions of administered doses,” Davidson said. “I want to emphasize that the evidence has found no increased risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth or birth defects. The risks of complications from Covid for pregnant people and their babies, however, are high. So please get the vaccine.” When to get it It’s recommended to get the updated vaccine now, but if you have been recently infected with Covid, experts advise waiting four to six months before getting the vaccine. The updated Covid-19 vaccine “targets the most recent strain that’s been circulating, and so if you want to update your protection, that’s the best way to do it,” Dr. Sandra Adamson Fryhofer, president-elect of the American Medical Association, said in a news briefing. “You know, your computer constantly needs to be updated. Well, your immune system, your immunity needs to be constantly updated too,” she said. “You’re going to get your most protection in those first few months after the vaccine. So if you have a big event – if you have to go to a wedding, or if you’re going on some fabulous trip, or you’re going to a fabulous birthday party, or just any birthday party or get-together – think about getting that vaccine a couple of weeks before that event, so you’ll stay healthy and well.”

content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 1-Oct-2026 COVID-19 immunity may help protect against other bat coronaviruses Study identifies links between virus host range and immune recognition Peer-Reviewed Publication The Pirbright Institute Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: A Rhinolophus bat. Photo courtesy of Bernard Agwanda, National Museums of Kenya. view more Credit: Bernard Agwanda, National Museums of Kenya People who recovered from COVID-19 infection or were vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2 are more likely to have immunity to other closely related bat coronaviruses that could have the potential to threaten future human health. In a joint study by The Pirbright Institute and King’s College London (KCL), scientists found bat coronaviruses most likely to infect a wide range of animal species are those most closely related to SARS-CoV-2 and most likely to be recognised by immunity generated through COVID-19 infection. The research, funded by the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (UK Research and Innovation - UKRI), Wellcome, and the Medical Research Council (MRC - part of UKRI), is published today in two companion articles in PLOS Biology. Researchers examined how a diverse group of bat sarbecoviruses - the coronavirus sub-group that includes SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 - interact with ACE2, the cellular receptor used by many coronaviruses to enter host cells. They investigated the ability of these viruses to use ACE2 proteins from a broad range of bat and mammalian species, including humans, livestock, rodents and animals previously proposed as intermediate hosts. The team discovered so-called "generalist" sarbecoviruses, which can use ACE2 receptors from many different species, were largely confined to the same evolutionary group as SARS-CoV-2. Pirbright postdoctoral scientist and lead author, Dr Nazia Thakur, said: "Our findings suggest that the bat coronaviruses currently considered most likely to spill over into humans are also most likely to be recognised by existing COVID-19 immunity. While spillover risk can never be eliminated, widespread exposure to SARS-CoV-2 may have raised the barrier for related viruses to establish themselves in human populations." The team analysed 15 representative bat coronavirus spike proteins using libraries of ACE2 receptors from 34 species. Broad ACE2 usage was a defining feature of viruses closely related to SARS-CoV-2, including the BANAL viruses discovered in Laos. Viruses from other evolutionary groups, including a novel UK bat coronavirus RhGB07, showed more restricted receptor usage. To aid in their analyses the Spike structure of RhGB07 was also resolved by collaborators in Switzerland. The study also investigated how SARS-CoV-2 host range has evolved during the pandemic. Researchers found variants, particularly those within the Omicron lineage acquired mutations in the receptor binding domain which resulted in shifting patterns of ACE2 usage across animal species, highlighting the dynamic relationship between viral evolution and host susceptibility. To understand the implications for human health, the scientists examined blood samples from people who had recovered from COVID-19. Antibodies in these samples successfully neutralised a range of closely related bat coronaviruses. Importantly, researchers also detected lower levels of neutralisation against more distant bat sarbecoviruses, suggesting some degree of broader protection. Katie Doores, Professor of Viral Immunology at KCL, said, “These viruses showed the strongest antigenic similarity to SARS-CoV-2, meaning they were more readily recognised and neutralised by antibodies generated following COVID-19 infection. In contrast, more distantly related bat coronaviruses tended to be "specialists", capable of using ACE2 receptors from only a limited range of hosts.” Further experiments at KCL and Pirbright identified several monoclonal antibodies capable of recognising a remarkably diverse range of sarbecoviruses. The second companion article identified where these monoclonal antibodies bind, highlighting conserved regions of the coronavirus spike protein, and offering important clues for the development of next-generation vaccines and therapeutics. Dr Dalan Bailey, head of Pirbright’s Viral Glycoproteins group, added: "One of the encouraging findings was evidence of cross-neutralisation of even some of the more distantly related bat coronaviruses. This suggests that broadly protective, pan-sarbecovirus vaccines or therapeutics may be achievable." The work highlights the importance of understanding virus host range, receptor usage and immune recognition together rather than in isolation. By identifying characteristics that distinguish higher-risk viruses from those less likely to spill over into humans, researchers hope to strengthen global pandemic preparedness efforts. content: 重症COVID-19 ICU患者清醒俯卧位(APP)反应因氧疗接口不同而异:一项前瞻性队列研究 《The Egyptian Journal of Critical Care Medicine》:Response to awake prone positioning in ICU patients with COVID-19 differs according to oxygenation interface: a prospective cohort study 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月03日 来源:The Egyptian Journal of Critical Care Medicine 0.3 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Original article Open access 背景:清醒俯卧位(APP)已广泛用于COVID-19相关急性呼吸窘迫综合征(ARDS)患者,但其有效性可能因氧疗接口而异。本研究旨在比较不同氧疗接口下对APP的反应,并识别反应预测因素。 方法:研究人员于2021年3月至5月开展前瞻性观察性研究,纳入因重型至危重型COVID-19入住重症监护病房(ICU)的成年患者。在入ICU后24 h内,使用常规氧疗(COT)、高流量鼻氧(HFNO)和无创通气(NIV)实施至少30 min的APP,并在可耐受时按序应用。每次APP前和APP后20 min测量动脉血气。反应定义为PaO 2 /FiO 2 比值增加≥20%。 结果:共纳入56例患者。不同接口反应率不同:COT下25.5%,HFNO下34.4%,NIV下43.9%。COT和HFNO下反应者插管率较低(p=0.03和p=0.01),HFNO下反应者住院时间较短(p=0.018)。除NIV外(p=0.6),所有接口下非反应者死亡率较高。较高的体质量指数(BMI)与COT和HFNO下的反应相关,受试者工作特征(ROC)分析识别出预测切点在27.3至28.3 kg/m2之间。 结论:对APP的反应因氧疗接口而异。APP反应可能与临床结局改善相关,尤其是在COT和HFNO下。较高的BMI似乎预测有利反应。鉴于观察性设计和接口序贯应用,这些发现应谨慎解释。 研究背景与问题 填写信息,下载 Twist FlexPrepTM UHT文库制备试剂盒产品详细技术资料 领 取 COVID-19(2019冠状病毒病)大流行导致急性呼吸窘迫综合征(ARDS,以急性低氧性呼吸衰竭为特征的临床综合征)发生率增加。俯卧位(PP)是ARDS机械通气患者早期管理中的体位干预;PROSEVA研究于2013年显示其可改善氧合、降低死亡率,机制包括改善支气管分泌物引流、降低右心室后负荷并增加前负荷。疫情期间,因需要重症监护的患者激增并对重症监护病房(ICU)容量造成显著压力,研究人员对非插管患者尝试清醒俯卧位(APP,非插管自主呼吸患者的俯卧位),以期改善氧合、预防插管并可能缩短住院时间。世界卫生组织(WHO)将重型COVID-19定义为肺炎临床征象伴呼吸窘迫(呼吸频率>30/min、室内空气下SpO 2 <90%),危重型COVID-19包括需要重症监护支持的ARDS、脓毒性休克或多器官衰竭患者。该区分重要,因为对APP等干预的生理反应可能随疾病严重度不同。既有研究支持APP改善自主呼吸呼吸衰竭患者氧合,包括因ARDS入住ICU者,但其降低插管率和死亡率的作用、耐受性及最佳持续时间仍不清楚。因此,本研究拟比较不同氧疗接口下APP反应,包括口插管需求、死亡和住院时间,并识别俯卧位反应预测因素。研究来源为TUNISIA的ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院。 研究人员开展什么研究、结论及意义 研究人员在ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院医疗ICU开展前瞻性观察性研究,纳入2021年3月至5月因COVID-19确诊重型至危重型(按WHO定义)入住、自主呼吸的成年患者。非纳入标准为患者拒绝俯卧位;排除标准为首次会话耐受差和/或临床情况严重恶化。研究人员收集人口学和临床数据,随访至出院,记录插管、插管时间和死亡。结论为:APP反应因氧疗接口不同;阳性反应可能与临床结局改善相关,尤其在常规氧疗(COT,通过鼻导管或面罩等常规给氧)和高流量鼻氧(HFNO,经鼻高流量氧疗)下;较高体质量指数(BMI,体重与身高平方之比)可能预测有利反应。意义在于提示APP应纳入阶梯式呼吸支持策略,HFNO可能在疗效与耐受之间较适合与APP联合,早期识别反应者可能有助于临床管理并避免延迟插管;但观察性设计、短时会话和接口序贯应用要求谨慎解释,需进一步随机研究证实。 关键技术方法 研究人员开展前瞻性观察性队列研究,队列来源为ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院医疗ICU,2021年3—5月因WHO定义重型至危重型COVID-19入住、自主呼吸的成年患者。纳入56例在入ICU 24 h内接受至少一次≥30 min APP者;COT、HFNO和无创通气(NIV,无需人工气道的正压通气)在可耐受时序贯应用。每次APP前后20 min在稳定氧合设置下行动脉血气,反应定义为动脉血氧分压/吸入氧分数比值(PaO 2 /FiO 2 )增加≥20%。收集插管、插管时间、死亡和住院时间。统计采用描述性分析、Student检验、卡方检验、趋势卡方检验、Kaplan-Meier与log-rank检验、受试者工作特征(ROC)曲线和曲线下面积(AUC)评估BMI预测价值,SPSS v23,P<0.05。 研究结果 入组与APP实施。研究期间117例因确诊SARS COV 2肺炎入住ICU,115例合格,56例接受至少一次>30 min APP。COT下51例,HFNO下32例,NIV下41例;COT反应率25.5%(n=13),HFNO 34.4%(n=11),NIV 43.9%(n=18)。全部患者至少在1种接口下接受俯卧位,32例为反应者;47例使用2种接口,其中8例为反应者;22例连续使用3种接口,其中2例为反应者。通过比较不同接口下APP前后PaO 2 /FiO 2 变化及反应率,研究人员得出反应因接口不同而异。 患者特征。多数为男性(n=41,72.5%),平均年龄55.9±15岁;在各接口下反应者与非反应者年龄多无差异,但1种接口反应者较非反应者年轻(52.13±15.8 vs 61±12.3,P=0.02)。平均BMI为28 kg/m2,在COT、HFNO、1种和2种接口反应者中更高(COT,p=0.01;HFNO,p=0.01;1种接口,p=0.03;2种接口,p=0.04)。高血压占24.6%(n=14),糖尿病占26.8%(n=15),各接口两组无差异。所有患者入院时均为ARDS,多为重度(45.1%)至中度(45.1%);胸部CT病变>75%者占15.2%,50%—75%者占50%,各接口两组无差异。入院PaO 2 在COT反应者中较低(66.9 vs 83.7,p=0.03)。平均耐受时间37 min,最大60 min,各组无差异。由此得出,高BMI和较低入院PaO 2 可能与某些接口下反应相关。 预后。插管率为42.9%(n=24),平均于入院后4天。COT非反应者机械通气需求显著更高(24[64.9] vs 4[30.8],p=0.03),1种接口组中非反应者也更高(反应者1[12.5] vs 非反应者24[61.5],p=0.01)。非反应者更多发生院内感染,尤其是呼吸机相关性肺炎(VAP)(HFNO非反应者50% vs 反应者9.1%,p=0.023;1种接口非反应者58% vs 反应者32%,p=0.04)。平均住院时间10±3天,HFNO反应者显著更短(9±3 vs 14±10天,p=0.018)。死亡率为46.4%(n=26),除NIV外(反应者38.9% vs 非反应者39%,p=0.6),所有接口非反应者死亡率更高。通过比较反应者与非反应者的插管、感染、住院时间和死亡,研究人员发现阳性反应在COT和HFNO下可能与较好临床结局相关。 BMI预测反应。由于COT、HFNO、1种和2种接口下反应者BMI显著更高,研究人员以ROC曲线寻找预测APP反应的BMI切点。结果BMI切点为27.3—28.3 kg/m2,AUC为0.68—0.82,敏感性为92.3%—65.6%,特异性为63.2%—71.4%。由此得出,较高BMI可能是某些接口下APP反应的预测因素。 讨论部分总结 讨论指出,在这一重症至危重型COVID-19 ICU患者前瞻性队列中,APP生理反应因氧疗接口不同:COT下较有限,HFNO下居中,NIV下较高。以APP后20 min PaO 2 /FiO 2 早期改善定义的阳性反应,在COT和HFNO下与较好临床结局相关,包括机械通气需求和死亡率,但在NIV下未显示。较高的BMI(切点27.3—28.3 kg/m2)可能是某些接口下反应的预测因素。研究人员分阶段从COT(无呼气末正压[PEEP])到HFNO(低PEEP)再到NIV(高PEEP)改变接口,并在入ICU 24 h内实施以减少疾病演变偏倚;短时30 min基于患者耐受和既往研究。反应定义20%与X.Elharrar等和Oliveira等一致,而文献中俯卧位反应定义异质。APP生理机制包括改善通气/灌注匹配、复张依赖肺区、减少肺内分流,这在COVID-19肺灌注失调和分流所致低氧中尤其相关。COT下APP似乎降低反应者死亡率,但未改善插管或住院时间;Padr?o等在急诊回顾队列中50例常规氧患者1—4 h俯卧位,50%患者SpO 2 /FiO 2 增加10%,APP对插管、无机械通气天数和死亡无益。接口差异具临床意义:COT无PEEP可能限制肺泡复张,HFNO提供低水平PEEP并减少解剖死腔,可能增强APP生理益处;这与Ehrmann等大型多中心meta试验显示APP显著减少HFNO患者插管需求一致,PROFLO随机临床试验也显示APP联合HFNO降低插管率和住院时间。尽管NIV反应率最高,但未转化为临床结局改善;这可能反映指征混杂,因NIV通常用于更严重呼吸衰竭患者,疾病严重度可能超过俯卧位益处;NIV俯卧位还可能患者-呼吸机不同步、面罩不耐受和呼吸功增加。高BMI与APP反应相关是本研究新发现,肥胖与功能残气量降低和仰卧位背侧肺压缩有关,俯卧位可能带来更大肺泡复张和氧合改善;近期meta分析提示超重和肥胖患者可能从俯卧位更多获益,但未定义具体预测阈值。研究优势为前瞻性比较不同接口下非插管清醒ICU患者APP反应。局限包括:接口序贯应用为非随机,是主要偏倚来源;反应定义为20 min短期氧合改善,可能不反映持续获益或长期结局;样本量较小,亚组分析可能降低统计效能并增加多重比较的I类错误风险;俯卧位平均37 min较短,可能限制获益;指南建议短时30 min至2 h每日重复,仍需更新包括APP启动资格、次数、每日平均时间、随访方案、并发症和失败早期识别及标准化插管标准。临床意义上,APP应整合入阶梯呼吸支持策略;鉴于疗效与耐受平衡,HFNO似乎最适合与APP联合;基于短期氧合改善和BMI早期识别反应者可能帮助临床医生调整管理并避免延迟插管;反之,无反应尤其在高阶支持如NIV下应促使重新评估并考虑有创机械通气。 研究结论翻译 短时间清醒俯卧位可行且安全。对清醒俯卧位的反应似乎因所用氧疗接口而异。阳性反应可能与结局改善相关,尤其是在常规氧疗和高流量鼻氧下。较高的BMI可能预测有利反应。由于观察性设计、俯卧时长较短和接口序贯应用,这些发现应谨慎解释。需要进一步随机研究证实这些结果。 研究背景与问题COVID-19(2019冠状病毒病)大流行导致急性呼吸窘迫综合征(ARDS,以急性低氧性呼吸衰竭为特征的临床综合征)发生率增加。俯卧位(PP)是ARDS机械通气患者早期管理中的体位干预;PROSEVA研究于2013年显示其可改善氧合、降低死亡率,机制包括改善支气管分泌物引流、降低右心室后负荷并增加前负荷。疫情期间,因需要重症监护的患者激增并对重症监护病房(ICU)容量造成显著压力,研究人员对非插管患者尝试清醒俯卧位(APP,非插管自主呼吸患者的俯卧位),以期改善氧合、预防插管并可能缩短住院时间。世界卫生组织(WHO)将重型COVID-19定义为肺炎临床征象伴呼吸窘迫(呼吸频率>30/min、室内空气下SpO<90%),危重型COVID-19包括需要重症监护支持的ARDS、脓毒性休克或多器官衰竭患者。该区分重要,因为对APP等干预的生理反应可能随疾病严重度不同。既有研究支持APP改善自主呼吸呼吸衰竭患者氧合,包括因ARDS入住ICU者,但其降低插管率和死亡率的作用、耐受性及最佳持续时间仍不清楚。因此,本研究拟比较不同氧疗接口下APP反应,包括口插管需求、死亡和住院时间,并识别俯卧位反应预测因素。研究来源为TUNISIA的ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院。研究人员开展什么研究、结论及意义研究人员在ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院医疗ICU开展前瞻性观察性研究,纳入2021年3月至5月因COVID-19确诊重型至危重型(按WHO定义)入住、自主呼吸的成年患者。非纳入标准为患者拒绝俯卧位;排除标准为首次会话耐受差和/或临床情况严重恶化。研究人员收集人口学和临床数据,随访至出院,记录插管、插管时间和死亡。结论为:APP反应因氧疗接口不同;阳性反应可能与临床结局改善相关,尤其在常规氧疗(COT,通过鼻导管或面罩等常规给氧)和高流量鼻氧(HFNO,经鼻高流量氧疗)下;较高体质量指数(BMI,体重与身高平方之比)可能预测有利反应。意义在于提示APP应纳入阶梯式呼吸支持策略,HFNO可能在疗效与耐受之间较适合与APP联合,早期识别反应者可能有助于临床管理并避免延迟插管;但观察性设计、短时会话和接口序贯应用要求谨慎解释,需进一步随机研究证实。关键技术方法研究人员开展前瞻性观察性队列研究,队列来源为ABDERRAHMANE MAMI医院医疗ICU,2021年3—5月因WHO定义重型至危重型COVID-19入住、自主呼吸的成年患者。纳入56例在入ICU 24 h内接受至少一次≥30 min APP者;COT、HFNO和无创通气(NIV,无需人工气道的正压通气)在可耐受时序贯应用。每次APP前后20 min在稳定氧合设置下行动脉血气,反应定义为动脉血氧分压/吸入氧分数比值(PaO/FiO)增加≥20%。收集插管、插管时间、死亡和住院时间。统计采用描述性分析、Student检验、卡方检验、趋势卡方检验、Kaplan-Meier与log-rank检验、受试者工作特征(ROC)曲线和曲线下面积(AUC)评估BMI预测价值,SPSS v23,P<0.05。研究结果入组与APP实施。研究期间117例因确诊SARS COV 2肺炎入住ICU,115例合格,56例接受至少一次>30 min APP。COT下51例,HFNO下32例,NIV下41例;COT反应率25.5%(n=13),HFNO 34.4%(n=11),NIV 43.9%(n=18)。全部患者至少在1种接口下接受俯卧位,32例为反应者;47例使用2种接口,其中8例为反应者;22例连续使用3种接口,其中2例为反应者。通过比较不同接口下APP前后PaO/FiO变化及反应率,研究人员得出反应因接口不同而异。患者特征。多数为男性(n=41,72.5%),平均年龄55.9±15岁;在各接口下反应者与非反应者年龄多无差异,但1种接口反应者较非反应者年轻(52.13±15.8 vs 61±12.3,P=0.02)。平均BMI为28 kg/m,在COT、HFNO、1种和2种接口反应者中更高(COT,p=0.01;HFNO,p=0.01;1种接口,p=0.03;2种接口,p=0.04)。高血压占24.6%(n=14),糖尿病占26.8%(n=15),各接口两组无差异。所有患者入院时均为ARDS,多为重度(45.1%)至中度(45.1%);胸部CT病变>75%者占15.2%,50%—75%者占50%,各接口两组无差异。入院PaO在COT反应者中较低(66.9 vs 83.7,p=0.03)。平均耐受时间37 min,最大60 min,各组无差异。由此得出,高BMI和较低入院PaO可能与某些接口下反应相关。预后。插管率为42.9%(n=24),平均于入院后4天。COT非反应者机械通气需求显著更高(24[64.9] vs 4[30.8],p=0.03),1种接口组中非反应者也更高(反应者1[12.5] vs 非反应者24[61.5],p=0.01)。非反应者更多发生院内感染,尤其是呼吸机相关性肺炎(VAP)(HFNO非反应者50% vs 反应者9.1%,p=0.023;1种接口非反应者58% vs 反应者32%,p=0.04)。平均住院时间10±3天,HFNO反应者显著更短(9±3 vs 14±10天,p=0.018)。死亡率为46.4%(n=26),除NIV外(反应者38.9% vs 非反应者39%,p=0.6),所有接口非反应者死亡率更高。通过比较反应者与非反应者的插管、感染、住院时间和死亡,研究人员发现阳性反应在COT和HFNO下可能与较好临床结局相关。BMI预测反应。由于COT、HFNO、1种和2种接口下反应者BMI显著更高,研究人员以ROC曲线寻找预测APP反应的BMI切点。结果BMI切点为27.3—28.3 kg/m,AUC为0.68—0.82,敏感性为92.3%—65.6%,特异性为63.2%—71.4%。由此得出,较高BMI可能是某些接口下APP反应的预测因素。讨论部分总结讨论指出,在这一重症至危重型COVID-19 ICU患者前瞻性队列中,APP生理反应因氧疗接口不同:COT下较有限,HFNO下居中,NIV下较高。以APP后20 min PaO/FiO早期改善定义的阳性反应,在COT和HFNO下与较好临床结局相关,包括机械通气需求和死亡率,但在NIV下未显示。较高的BMI(切点27.3—28.3 kg/m)可能是某些接口下反应的预测因素。研究人员分阶段从COT(无呼气末正压[PEEP])到HFNO(低PEEP)再到NIV(高PEEP)改变接口,并在入ICU 24 h内实施以减少疾病演变偏倚;短时30 min基于患者耐受和既往研究。反应定义20%与X.Elharrar等和Oliveira等一致,而文献中俯卧位反应定义异质。APP生理机制包括改善通气/灌注匹配、复张依赖肺区、减少肺内分流,这在COVID-19肺灌注失调和分流所致低氧中尤其相关。COT下APP似乎降低反应者死亡率,但未改善插管或住院时间;Padr?o等在急诊回顾队列中50例常规氧患者1—4 h俯卧位,50%患者SpO/FiO增加10%,APP对插管、无机械通气天数和死亡无益。接口差异具临床意义:COT无PEEP可能限制肺泡复张,HFNO提供低水平PEEP并减少解剖死腔,可能增强APP生理益处;这与Ehrmann等大型多中心meta试验显示APP显著减少HFNO患者插管需求一致,PROFLO随机临床试验也显示APP联合HFNO降低插管率和住院时间。尽管NIV反应率最高,但未转化为临床结局改善;这可能反映指征混杂,因NIV通常用于更严重呼吸衰竭患者,疾病严重度可能超过俯卧位益处;NIV俯卧位还可能患者-呼吸机不同步、面罩不耐受和呼吸功增加。高BMI与APP反应相关是本研究新发现,肥胖与功能残气量降低和仰卧位背侧肺压缩有关,俯卧位可能带来更大肺泡复张和氧合改善;近期meta分析提示超重和肥胖患者可能从俯卧位更多获益,但未定义具体预测阈值。研究优势为前瞻性比较不同接口下非插管清醒ICU患者APP反应。局限包括:接口序贯应用为非随机,是主要偏倚来源;反应定义为20 Politics Money Arts Justice Environment Newsletter Ways to support Gov. Jared Polis gets vaccinated to protect against flu and COVID-19 By John Daley · Oct. 1, 2026, 6:44 pm Share: Kevin J. Beaty/Denverite Lauren Brown, a registered nurse and supervisor with the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment's Mobile Public Health Clinic, gives Gov. Jared Polis his annual flu and COVID vaccinations in his office at the Colorado State Capitol. Oct. 1, 2026. With flu numbers in Colorado starting to mount, Gov. Jared Polis got vaccinated in his office at the Capitol Thursday. He rolled up his sleeves (but not too far, he was wearing a short sleeved shirt) for two shots: one for flu and one for COVID-19. “Just trying to lead by example here and show other Coloradans how easy this is. You barely feel these things,” he said as he smiled for a photo. Nearly 7% of Coloradans have already gotten their flu shot, according to the state health department. That’s a decrease of more than 1% from this time last year. More than 6-thousand Coloradans were hospitalized with flu over the past year, according to the state’s viral respiratory disease dashboard. At Christmas last year, hospitals were jammed with a record number of flu patients who needed to be admitted — nearly 800 by New Year’s Eve. Polis said he gets the shots both for himself and other folks he spends time with. “My parents are in their 80s and I want to reduce the chance that I get something,” he said. “They've already gotten theirs, so I'm excited to reduce the chance that I'll be out of commission for a while or spread these to other people I know.” Vaccines for flu, updated COVID shots and RSV are available at pharmacies, clinics and doctors' offices. Last season, about a third of Coloradans got vaccinated for flu, which was a bit lower than the year before. Less than 14 percent of Colorado residents got a COVID-19 immunization, according to the state, which was lower than the year before. Doctors and major medical groups say getting vaccinated is the best way to avoid serious illness from these viruses. And it appears more flu cases are brewing in Colorado. “We have been seeing a flurry of activity much before we anticipated. We're starting to see flu cases much before that we typically see around November or December of each year,” said Dr. Edwin Asturias, a pediatric infectious disease physician at the Colorado School of Public Health. This is a good time, he said, for people to be ready for the flu season that comes as soon as the vaccine is already here. “I think we may have an earlier season than other years in the past,” said Asturias, a former member of the U.S. Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. The state health department's viral respiratory dashboard showed 36 people are now hospitalized with flu, as of the end of September. A month ago there was only one. Additionally, 34 people were hospitalized with COVID. UCHealth infectious diseases expert Dr. Michelle Barron said her health system saw four times as many positive flu cases in September than the same month last year. “So, flu is already circulating,” she said. She said now is a good time to get your shots, just as the governor did Thursday. “Anyone over 6 months of age should get a flu and COVID shot. I would strongly recommend the very young and the very old,” she said. She defined that loosely as anyone over 65. She said pregnant women should also get their shots, because they're also very susceptible to flu and COVID. You care. You want to know what is really going on these days, especially in Colorado. We can help you keep up. The Lookout is a free, daily email newsletter with news and happenings from all over Colorado. Sign up here and we will see you in the morning! Business Guide Hub Communications All News Academics Planning for the future: St. Mike’s group explores what worked (and didn’t) during VT’s COVID-19 response by Rylee Anderson '27 October 2, 2026 Share From left, past Saint Michael's College research student Elsa Gordon poses with current researchers Emily Gates and Damascene Niyongere after presenting on their research through the SOCKS grant. (Courtesy of Candas Pinar) October 2, 2026 Rylee Anderson '27 Vermont is considered to have had one of the most successful responses to the COVID-19 pandemic in the U.S. when the virus brought the world to a standstill in 2020. A research group at St. Mike’s is asking why. Over the past four years, the multidisciplinary project has given students real-world research experience while allowing faculty to explore effective communication strategies in hopes of limiting the effects of future public health emergencies. This past summer, a group of undergraduates worked on the project alongside Sociology Professor Candas Pinar, Computer Science Professor Bradford Demarest, and Political Science and Public Health Professor Patricia Siplon. They are particularly interested in Gov. Phil Scott’s press conferences from that time, beginning in March 2020. They are analyzing Scott’s speeches and answers to reporters’ questions through multiple lenses, including public health. Vermont Gov. Phil Scott gives a press conference, which was streamed by ORCA Media, in March 2020 explaining the “Stay Home, Stay Safe” initiative to prevent the spread of COVID-19. Saint Michael’s College professors and students are currently several years into a five-year grant to study why Scott’s messaging was so effective in Vermont. The research is part of the University of Vermont’s broader Science of Online Corpora, Knowledge, and Stories (SOCKS) project, which is federally funded through Vermont EPSCoR (The Vermont Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research). While the analysis methods vary among the members of the Saint Michael’s team, they’re all focused on the same question: whether Scott’s language called on social capital and how that affected Vermonters’ actions during the pandemic. Social capital, at its core, is what holds communities together. Pinar explained that it is “the connections and bonds that exist between people. “It’s also what we have access to as a result of those bonds,” Pinar added. “We might get access to new information, or if you live in a community where people look out for each other, you might enjoy a higher level of security.” The team is looking through transcripts from videos of Phil Scott’s speeches to dial in on when and how he references this kind of ideology. Saint Michael’s College faculty and students discuss progress they’ve made so far on research into Vermont Gov. Phil Scott’s COVID-19 messaging and why it was so effective in the state. (Courtesy of Candas Pinar) Studying stories and social capital The SOCKS project, in essence, aims to study words and stories, and their power. These researchers are studying how Gov. Scott used stories and specific language during COVID-19 press conferences to bring communities together and encourage adherence to health guidelines. The project began with Pinar and Siplon partnering with former Saint Michael’s Criminology Professor Krista Billingsley, who served as the project’s Primary Investigator (PI). Demarest later joined the group, and Pinar took over as the PI after Billingsley pursued new opportunities beyond the College. “We were really interested in Vermont’s response to the COVID- 19 pandemic, because it was such a leader in this country,” Pinar said. “We knew that Vermont is known for being a state that has a very coherent sense of community, and very high levels of what we call social capital. So, we brought those two interests together into this project where we were wondering, to what extent did political leaders in Vermont during the pandemic really highlight those stories of community in their communications with the public?” Social capital is a major topic in the social sciences, specifically sociology, but to others, it’s an elusive term. When she first joined the SOCKS team, Health Science major Clara Hershey ’28 was unfamiliar with the concept. “I’ve never taken a sociology class,” Hershey said. Social capital, she added, was “the bulk of what our research team was focused on. I did a lot of reading the literature and trying to grasp what social capital was.” From left, past Saint Michael’s College research student Elsa Gordon poses with current researchers Emily Gates and Damascene Niyongere after presenting on their research through the SOCKS project. (Courtesy of Candas Pinar) The grant began at the tail end of the pandemic, and Pinar said that “it was the forefront of a lot of what we were doing as public health professors.” The research continued this summer, with six students involved. Emily Gates ’27 has been working with Pinar for the past two summers, while Lavender Gaudette ’27 and Hershey joined the team this year. Maya Clough ’28, who is also working on research with Chemistry Professor Megan Browning, has helped collect data for the team by transcribing the press conference videos into text that they could analyze. “All of the data that we’re working with has to be created,” Pinar said. “That requires a very elaborate and tedious process that Maya has spearheaded this summer. The original data set was created by another undergrad, but because of Maya’s contributions, we now have language from press conferences before the COVID-19 pandemic so that we can compare over time.” Comparing press conference language before and during the pandemic is just one way the project is constantly growing and evolving. The team is also analyzing Scott’s speeches against those of Chris Sununu, New Hampshire’s governor during the pandemic. Using computational linguistics to dig deeper Technology is playing an important role in this research, with Computer Science Professor Demarest bringing his expertise into the equation. “My focus is on computational linguistics, those tools that are more quantitative,” Demarest said. “Like trying to get a general description of a great pile of text so people can do things like noticing just where he’s talking about Vermonters instead of having to go through with a fine-tooth comb.” Saint Michael’s Professors Trish Siplon (Political Science and Public Health), Candas Pinar (Sociology), and Bradford Demarest (Computer Science) pose for a photo together at the New England Political Science Association’s conference. (Photo courtesy of Candas Pinar) Samantha Galle ’29 worked under Demarest’s mentorship this summer, and, like Demarest, comes from a background in linguistics. “I’m learning the more technical side of it,” Galle said. “I feel like you can’t fully understand how something works, even if you’re zeroed in on a particular subject like we are, unless you look at it from multiple different angles that seem to have no correlation.” Learning tools like Python and using the SOCKS “Hedonometer” instrument, which measures the happiness of large populations over time by analyzing social media data, Demarest and Galle have been diving deeper into the language Scott used in his speeches. The tools help them determine whether words are “good” or “bad,” “happy” or “unhappy,” and how they relate to other words. “We found there’s a strong correlation between ‘goodness’ and ‘power,’ as well as a strong negative correlation between ‘goodness’ and ‘danger,’” Galle said. “We gathered all this data, but we can’t really make sense of it just yet until we compare it to a control, which will be transcripts from a non-COVID-era press conference that Phil Scott has done.” The research continues into the school year, as the grant covers a five-year period. Looking at where Vermont was lacking Political Science and Public Health Professor Siplon is probing another question in this same vein with the help of Damascene Niyongere ’27, another student who has been part of this project for two summers. They are looking at where Vermont and Scott didn’t do as well, namely the impact of COVID-19 on the incarceration system. “What we’re looking at is how Vermont did or didn’t use the same social capital approach with regard to its incarceration system,” Siplon said. Like many other states, Vermont had to come up with sets of policies and ways of dealing with people who were incarcerated during the pandemic. The incarceration system was one of the highest-risk areas in the state since, like nursing homes, it housed groups of at-risk people in close quarters. “Vermont doesn’t have the capacity to house all of its incarcerated people in the state, so it essentially outsourced people, and their experience was pretty bad,” Siplon said, alluding to the state’s longtime practice of sending incarcerated people to prisons outside Vermont. “We’re looking at both the policies themselves and how those policies were, and sometimes weren’t, talked about.” Damascene Niyongere ’27 speaks at the annual summer research kickoff brunch at Saint Michael’s in summer 2026, describing the work he’s doing through the SOCKS project with Political Science and Public Health Professor Trish Siplon. (Photo by Christina Cummings ’25) Niyongere and Siplon reviewed reports from the Vermont Department of Corrections, public health literature, state policies, and news coverage to discover the impact of COVID-19 on Vermont’s six correctional facilities. Incarcerated individuals were placed in quarantine when exposed to the virus, and the group sought to find out how this affected the people in the facilities. “While quarantine was an important control measure, our research found that prolonged isolation contributed to increased anxiety, depression, loneliness, and worsened mental health,” Niyongere said. The research also found higher transmission rates in state correctional facilities, with nearly 70% of those tested in 2020 being found positive for the virus. “This research showed that Vermont failed to uphold the same level of concern for social capital of incarcerated people that they showed in the general population,” Niyongere explained. A ‘multi-year, multi-disciplinary, multi-level’ project This research has been a long and winding journey, but at its core, it reflects the values of Saint Michael’s College, particularly the close student-professor collaboration that occurs on campus. “That’s why I’m at a place like Saint Michael’s,” Pinar said. “I love the fact that I can work on this project and have people just to check in with. It’s so much more fun and positive, and I think it produces better science, honestly.” The students, like the faculty working on the project, each bring a unique perspective to the table. From Gates, a Digital Media & Marketing and Sociology/Anthropology double major, to Hershey, a Health Sciences major, the students are branching out beyond their academic disciplines to experience real-world research with myriad applications. “Being on a research team, I’ve been able to see and experience the process of troubleshooting and backtracking,” Hershey said. “It’s really my first experience doing research like this, and I’ve been able to understand how do you pivot in a different direction? How do you look at something differently?” Like any research group, the team faced challenges. Galle, who came from a linguistics background, had to learn new computer science tools before using them for the project, which made for less efficient results. Pinar’s team, including Gates, Hershey, and Gaudette, had to decide whether to double down on explicit social capital references or include inferred references. They also moved away from using the CDC’s Tool for Thematic Analysis and found new tools that worked best for their research. However, despite these challenges, the group still gained valuable research experience and is working toward finishing the final two years of the research grant. They hope their research will provide valuable information about governments’ emergency responses. “If and when there’s another pandemic, we can take what we learned about effective communication strategies that help to build common ground among people,” Pinar said. “But the work extends beyond pandemics. You can think about any emergency situation.” For example, Pinar said more climate-related human-generated disasters are likely scenarios that societies will need to face in the future. “Learning as much as we can about communication strategies that can create an effective, collective response is really important,” she said. Students had the opportunity to present their research at the University of Vermont last spring, and they hope to present at another conference in New Hampshire in October. “We have our own little community in its fourth year, and we have great student researchers, and also alumni who have come out of the program interested in what’s going on and in taking their skills into other places,” Siplon said. “This is my 29th year at St. Mike’s, and this is the first time that I’ve been in a multi-year, multi-disciplinary, multi-level project like this. It feels really special for me.” For all press inquiries contact Elizabeth Murray, Associate Director of Communications at Saint Michael's College. content: News Sports Business Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Your guide to vaccines for flu, COVID-19 and RSV in Wisconsin Madeline Heim Milwaukee Journal Sentinel Oct. 1, 2026, 5:05 a.m. CT The Wisconsin Department of Health Services released annual recommendations for flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines for this fall. Flu and COVID-19 vaccines are recommended for residents 6 months and older, especially those most at risk of severe illness. One dose of the RSV is recommended for all adults 75 and older, some 50 and older and during 32-36 weeks of pregnancy. Local physicians say they are glad to field questions from their patients about which vaccines to take and when. It's officially fall – leaves are turning, evening sunlight is fading, and respiratory viruses will soon start circulating at higher levels. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Sept. 30 released its annual recommendations for vaccines to protect against the flu and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, as well as updated COVID-19 shots. The recommendations lean on guidance from major medical organizations, not the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose immunization committee is currently inactive due to federal turmoil around vaccines and is not expected to issue updated guidelines. Across Wisconsin, about 11,000 people were hospitalized during last year's respiratory season with the flu, COVID-19 or RSV, chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases Dr. Ryan Westergaard said in a Sept. 30 news briefing. "That's something that you wouldn't wish on anyone," he said. Dr. Bill Calawerts, a family medicine physician and assistant professor at the Medical College of Wisconsin, said he welcomes discussions about which vaccines are appropriate and when. "I and my physician colleagues are not offended by questions," Calawerts said. "If you really want to talk about it, don't be ashamed to bring questions to your clinician." Vaccines for respiratory viruses are covered by most insurance plans and are available at doctors' offices, local health departments, pharmacies and pop-up vaccine clinics. Those who need help paying for vaccines can use the Vaccines for Children and Vaccines for Adults programs. Here's what you need to know about the shots available in Wisconsin this fall. Updated COVID-19 vaccine The state health department recommends that all residents ages 6 months and older receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine. These vaccines are being updated yearly to target the latest strains of the virus. The vaccine is especially recommended for adults 65 and older, as well as others who are more likely to become seriously ill from contracting COVID-19. COVID-19 vaccines are most effective for the first three months after receiving the shot, offering protection against serious illness. Last year, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. retracted the recommendation for healthy children and pregnant people to receive the COVID-19 vaccine, a move that has since been temporarily blocked by a federal judge. Such changes caused people to be unsure of whether their insurer would cover the shot. Wisconsin health officials issued guidance still broadly supporting the vaccine, but not many people got it. Less than 14% of residents got an updated COVID-19 vaccine during the 2025-26 respiratory virus season, immunization data show. Seniors were the most likely to receive it, with more than one in three people 65 and older getting the updated shot. This year, federal health officials delayed COVID-19 vaccine doses available through the Vaccines for Children program, which offers free vaccines to the uninsured or underinsured. Wisconsin's allocation was delayed, Westergaard confirmed, but eventually arrived, and Vaccines for Children providers were able to start ordering doses Sept. 28. Orders for about 5,000 doses have been filled already, he said. Calawerts said he is still recommending the COVID-19 vaccine to most of his patients. "I describe it like wearing a helmet when you're riding a bike. That's only really your personal choice, how much risk you're willing to take, and ultimately it's totally your decision to make as well," Calawerts said. "It's an extra layer of protection if you get an infection." COVID-19 activity in Wisconsin is currently very low, according to state respiratory virus data. Flu vaccine State health officials recommend everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine, especially older adults, people with chronic conditions, young children and pregnant people. Already, the state is seeing a slight increase in influenza cases, Westergaard said. The flu is difficult for scientists to prepare for, and each year, they try to predict what type of vaccine will offer the most protection against it. That means it's not always a perfect match. Last year, for example, the shot didn't protect as well against a new strain of the virus that emerged. Calawerts said he's up front with his patients about that, but still points out that the flu vaccine is meant to lower risk of severe complications. Studies have shown the flu vaccine can significantly reduce people's risk of severe outcomes if they contract the disease. This year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a new type of flu vaccine called mFLUSIVA for use in people 50 and older. It's the first flu vaccine to use mRNA technology, similar to some COVID-19 vaccines. In clinical trials, the vaccine was about 27% more effective at preventing influenza than a traditional flu vaccine. The mRNA flu vaccine will be available in Wisconsin, Westergaard said, but only through private providers, and it may not be covered by all insurance plans for people 50 to 64. "It's a newer tool in our toolkit, so this season might be one where uptake is lower than others," he said. "The data appear to be very favorable in terms of effectiveness and safety so far." The number of Wisconsin residents getting the flu vaccine has been falling since the pandemic. Last season, about one in three residents of all ages received it. Experts say it is safe to receive the flu vaccine and COVID-19 vaccine at the same time. They recommend getting the flu shot by the end of October. RSV vaccine Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, causes cold-like symptoms and is usually mild in adults and older healthy children. In infants, older adults and people with heart or lung diseases, it can be more serious. The state health department recommends a one-time dose of the RSV for people over 50 who are at increased risk of severe disease, for all adults 75 and older, and during 32-36 weeks of pregnancy between Sept. 1 and March 1. If the RSV vaccine isn't given during pregnancy, health officials recommend an RSV antibody shot for infants younger than 8 months. The RSV vaccine can be given at the same time as other vaccines. As of Sept. 23, nearly 19% of Wisconsin residents 50 and older have received an RSV vaccine, according to state immunization data, and about 36% of residents 75 and older. Last respiratory virus season, close to 26,800 doses of antibody to protect against RSV were administered to Wisconsin infants, the state health department said. RSV activity in Wisconsin is currently very low. Madeline Heim covers health and the environment for the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. Contact her at 920-996-7266 or mheim@usatodayco.com. Wisconsin's allocation was delayed, Westergaard confirmed, but eventually arrived, and Vaccines for Children providers were able to start ordering doses Sept. 28. Orders for about 5,000 doses have been filled already, he said. Calawerts said he is still recommending the COVID-19 vaccine to most of his patients. "I describe it like wearing a helmet when you're riding a bike. That's only really your personal choice, how much risk you're willing to take, and ultimately it's totally your decision to make as well," Calawerts said. "It's an extra layer of protection if you get an infection." COVID-19 activity in Wisconsin is currently very low, according to state respiratory virus data. Flu vaccine State health officials recommend everyone 6 months and older get a flu vaccine, especially older adults, people with chronic conditions, young children and pregnant people. Already, the state is seeing a slight increase in influenza cases, Westergaard said. The flu is difficult for scientists to prepare for, and each year, they try to predict what type of vaccine will offer the most protection against it. That means it's not always a perfect match. Last year, for example, the shot didn't protect as well against a new strain of the virus that emerged. Calawerts said he's up front with his patients about that, but still points out that the flu vaccine is meant to lower risk of severe complications. Studies have shown the flu vaccine can significantly reduce people's risk of severe outcomes if they contract the disease. This year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a new type of flu vaccine called mFLUSIVA for use in people 50 and older. It's the first flu vaccine to use mRNA technology, similar to some COVID-19 vaccines. In clinical trials, the vaccine was about 27% more effective at preventing influenza than a traditional flu vaccine. The mRNA flu vaccine will be available in Wisconsin, Westergaard said, but only through private providers, and it may not be covered by all insurance plans for people 50 to 64. "It's a newer tool in our toolkit, so this season might be one where uptake is lower than others," he said. "The data appear to be very favorable in terms of effectiveness and safety so far." The number of Wisconsin residents getting the flu vaccine has been falling since the pandemic. Last season, about one in three residents of all ages received it. Experts say it is safe to receive the flu vaccine and COVID-19 vaccine at the same time. They recommend getting the flu shot by the end of October. RSV vaccine Respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, causes cold-like symptoms and is usually mild in adults and older healthy children. In infants, older adults and people with heart or lung diseases, it can be more serious. The state health department recommends a one-time dose of the RSV for people over 50 who are at increased risk of severe disease, for all adults 75 and older, and during 32-36 weeks of pregnancy between Sept. 1 and March 1. If the RSV vaccine isn't given during pregnancy, health officials recommend an RSV antibody shot for infants younger than 8 months. The RSV vaccine can be given at the same time as other vaccines. As of Sept. 23, nearly 19% of Wisconsin residents 50 and older have received an RSV vaccine, according to state immunization data, and about 36% of residents 75 and older. Last respiratory virus season, close to 26,800 doses of antibody to protect against RSV were administered to Wisconsin infants, the state health department said. RSV activity in Wisconsin is currently very low. Madeline Heim covers health and the environment for the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. Contact her at 920-996-7266 or mheim@usatodayco.com. content_title: Magnetic Stimulation Improves Long COVID “Brain Fog”
content: The therapy proved safe, well tolerated, and easily administered by patients remotely at home. Credit: Neuroscience News Magnetic Stimulation Improves Long COVID “Brain Fog” FeaturedNeurologyNeuroscience ·September 30, 2026 Summary: A pilot clinical trial led by the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai shows that an at-home, non-invasive magnetic headset significantly improves cognitive performance and emotional well-being in adults suffering from long COVID “brain fog.” Published in Brain Communications, the triple-blind, sham-controlled study found that twice-weekly sessions of Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT) enhanced working memory, processing speed, and verbal learning, with therapeutic benefits persisting a full month after treatment ended. Key Facts: Targeted Brain Stimulation: Participants self-administered 15-minute sessions twice weekly for four weeks using an investigational headset delivering nonthermal radio-frequency low-amplitude magnetic fields (MMT) to the whole brain. Measurable Cognitive & Mood Gains: Active treatment produced significant gains in working memory, processing speed, verbal learning, and self-reported emotional well-being compared to an identical sham device. Durable Aftereffects: Cognitive improvements continued between the end of the four-week treatment window and the eight-week follow-up assessment, indicating lasting neuroplastic or anti-inflammatory changes. Source: Mount Sinai Health System Among the constellation of symptoms defining post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), commonly termed long COVID, cognitive dysfunction remains among the most debilitating. Millions of individuals describe a persistent “brain fog” characterized by slowed processing speed, executive dysfunction, working memory lapses, and attention deficits that derail employment and daily life. Emerging neuropathological evidence indicates that long COVID cognitive deficits stem from a combination of sustained neuroinflammation, microvascular endotheliopathy, and mitochondrial metabolic exhaustion within neural tissue. Yet, despite the vast global disease burden, clinically validated therapeutic interventions remain exceedingly rare. In a randomized, triple-blind pilot trial published in Brain Communications, investigators from the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai evaluated whether biophysical neuromodulation could counter these entrenched post-viral neurological symptoms. The researchers tested Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT), a proprietary, non-invasive technology developed by clinical-stage biophysics company Fareon® that delivers low-amplitude, nonthermal radio-frequency magnetic fields across the cortex. “Cognitive symptoms are among the most persistent and disabling manifestations of long COVID, yet evidence-based treatment options have been sparse,” said co-senior author Jacqueline Becker, Ph.D., clinical neuropsychologist and assistant professor of medicine at Icahn Mount Sinai. “What is particularly encouraging about these findings is that we observed improvements across several cognitive domains, as well as in daily functioning and well-being, and that these improvements persisted even after treatment ended.” Triple-Blind, At-Home Intervention The clinical trial enrolled 30 adults with objectively documented post-COVID cognitive impairment. Participants were randomized 2:1 to receive either active MMT or an indistinguishable sham treatment that looked, sounded, and operated identically. Subjects wore the headset at home for 15 minutes twice a week over a four-week period, monitored remotely by Mount Sinai clinical trial coordinators. The investigators assessed cognitive performance, mood, and quality-of-life metrics at baseline, at week four (conclusion of the intervention), and at week eight (four-week post-treatment follow-up). The home-administered protocol proved safe, feasible, and well tolerated, with participants exceeding the 80% protocol completion threshold without significant device-related adverse events. Patients receiving active MMT demonstrated marked improvements in objective neuropsychological endpoints, including: Working Memory: Enhanced capacity to retain and manipulate information over short intervals. Processing Speed: Increased cognitive reaction time and task execution speed. Verbal Learning: Stronger retention and recall during verbal memory tasks. Emotional Well-Being: Reductions in mood disturbance and gains in self-reported daily quality of life. Lasting Neuroplastic Improvements Beyond Treatment Critically, the therapeutic gains did not diminish when patients took off the headset at the end of week four. During the subsequent four-week washout observation period, participants in the active cohort exhibited continued cognitive and mood improvements through week eight. While the primary mechanisms remain under investigation, preclinical models of MMT indicate that low-amplitude magnetic oscillations can suppress chronic neuroinflammation, downregulate reactive microglial activation, and support mitochondrial bioenergetics, biological pathways known to be compromised in post-viral encephalopathies. “According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, roughly 7 percent of Americans are experiencing symptoms related to long COVID, and a majority of these people report cognitive symptoms as amongst their most troubling and disabling symptoms,” said co-senior author David Putrino, Ph.D., Nash Family Director of the Cohen Center for Recovery From Complex Chronic Illness at Icahn Mount Sinai. “There is an urgent need to find answers and effective treatments for the hundreds of millions of people worldwide who are struggling with long COVID. This first-in-human study is a promising start for a completely novel therapy that is showing great potential.” The researchers emphasize that while these initial pilot results are promising, MMT remains an investigational therapy that requires verification in larger multicenter cohorts to determine optimal dosage schedules, long-term durability, and the exact biological mechanisms restoring network function. Editorial Notes: This article was edited by a Neuroscience News editor. Journal paper reviewed in full. Additional context added by our staff. About this neurotech and long COVID Research: Media Contact: Elizabeth Dowling Source: Mount Sinai Hospital Image Credit: Image credited to Neuroscience News Original Research is Open Access: Brain Communications (Sept 22, 2026). “Microtesla magnetic therapy for cognitive impairment in long COVID: a randomized pilot study.” Authors: Alexandra Canori, PhD , Eric Watson, PhD , Devanshi Patel, MA , Arianna Fiorentino, MSc , Christopher Santiago, BS , David Maltz, MSE , Blake Gurfein, PhD , David Putrino, PhD , Jacqueline Becker, PhD. DOI: 10.1093/braincomms/fcag364 Abstract Microtesla magnetic therapy for cognitive impairment in long COVID: a randomized pilot study Cognitive impairment is common in post-acute sequelae of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 infection (long COVID) and substantially affects function and quality of life. Evidence suggests that sustained neuroinflammation, cerebrovascular dysfunction, and mitochondrial impairment contribute to cognitive symptoms. Microtesla Magnetic Therapy (MMT) is a transcranial, low-amplitude radiofrequency magnetic field intervention that has shown anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in preclinical models, suggesting potential value in long COVID and other neurological disorders. This is the first randomized controlled trial of MMT for long COVID cognitive impairment. Join our Newsletter Thank you for subscribing. Something went wrong.
