COVID-19 was associated with increased risks of all six allergic conditions in the full cohort. Findings highlighted the potential value of monitoring for allergic disease after COVID-19. COVID-19 infection was associated with an increased risk of six newly diagnosed allergic conditions in a retrospective cohort study of children and adults aged 1–64 years. The findings highlighted a potential allergic disease burden following infection, with different patterns observed in children and active-duty service members. Assessing Allergic Disease After COVID-19 Researchers conducted a retrospective cohort study using 1:2 propensity score matching to evaluate the association between COVID-19 exposure and the development of allergic conditions over 18 months. The outcomes were atopic dermatitis, asthma, food allergy, rhinoconjunctivitis, medication allergy, and urticaria. The analysis focused on incident conditions, examining new diagnoses during follow-up. Researchers calculated hazard ratios for each outcome across the full cohort and conducted separate analyses in children and active-duty service members. These subgroup analyses examined whether the associations observed across the study population were also present in these groups. Associations Differ Between Population Groups In the full cohort, COVID-19 infection was associated with significantly increased hazard ratios for all six allergic conditions. The findings therefore extended across respiratory, skin, food, and medication-related outcomes rather than being confined to a single diagnosis. Among active-duty service members, statistically significant associations were observed for asthma and rhinoconjunctivitis. In children, infection was significantly associated with five of the six conditions, with food allergy being the exception. Higher sponsor rank, assessed as a potential surrogate for socioeconomic status, was associated with a slightly lower risk of developing asthma. This association provided an additional finding concerning socioeconomic circumstances, although sponsor rank represented a proxy measure. Clinical Implications of Allergic Disease Risk The findings added to evidence of an association between COVID-19 infection and subsequent allergic disease in both children and adults. The authors emphasised the potential public health burden and the importance of monitoring for allergic conditions after infection to support prompt intervention. They also suggested a possible mechanistic link between COVID-19 and type two inflammation. However, the retrospective observational design means that the reported associations do not establish causation or confirm the proposed inflammatory mechanism. Reference: Clarion J et al. Post–COVID-19 onset of allergic conditions in a propensity-matched cohort of children and adults. Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol. 2026;137(2):185–193.e2. The coronavirus disease, COVID-19, has continued to spread around the world. The disease has reached more than 200 countries. Only one country in the world has not yet reported cases of the virus . There have now been around 657.7 million cases, and more than 6,679,900 deaths reported around the world. Though the news has been mainly focused on the very serious problems caused by the disease, it’s important to remember that many people who get the illness don’t have serious effects. Most people who get the disease get better. Each country is testing and reporting its numbers in its own way. This means that comparing numbers for different countries may not give a true picture of how the disease is actually spreading. China was the first country to face a large outbreak of COVID-19. content: Wednesday, September 30, 2026 Your care team can help you decide which vaccines to get and when. Flu, RSV, and COVID-19 are common illnesses caused by viruses. They tend to spread more in the fall and winter. Getting vaccinated lowers your risk of getting sick. If you do get sick, being vaccinated also lowers your risk of serious illness. Cancer and cancer treatment can weaken your immune system, which is your body’s defense against infection. This is called being immunocompromised. When your immune system is weakened, it’s harder for your body to fight off these viruses, and they’re more likely to make you very sick. Learn more about each vaccine Our experts answer common questions about each one. What to know about the flu Five myths about the flu shot RSV vaccines: Who can get one, side effects, and getting one at MSK COVID-19 vaccines for people with cancer or a weakened immune system Back to top Which vaccines should I get? It depends on your age, health, and treatment. Talk with your care team. They’ll tell you which vaccines to get and the best time to get them. Back to top Where can I get my vaccines? You can get them at MSK. Just ask your care team. You can also get them at most pharmacies. Back to top Should the people I live with get vaccinated too? Yes. When the people in your home and close circle get vaccinated, it helps protect both you and them. Encourage your family, caregivers, and close friends to stay up to date on their vaccines. content_title: COVID-19 Drops Out Of World’s Top 10 Causes Of Death For First Time Since Pandemic Began - Health Policy Watch
content: COVID dropped out of the 10 leading causes of deaths, while noncommunicable diseases caused 74% of deaths worldwide in 2023. COVID-19 dropped out of the world’s 10 leading causes of death in 2023 for the first time since the pandemic began in 2020, and only two years after it topped the list, according to new World Health Organization estimates released Friday. The virus directly killed an estimated 0.9 million people in 2023, ranking 14th, as global life expectancy climbed back to near its pre-pandemic level. WHO declared an end to COVID-19 as a global health emergency in May that year. Revised figures now rank COVID-19 as the world’s leading cause of death in 2021, with 9.4 million direct deaths. WHO’s earlier estimates had placed it second that year. Together with 5.3 million deaths in 2020, the new figures put the virus’s direct toll in the first two years of the pandemic at 14.7 million. Figures WHO published in 2024, based on an earlier round of estimates, showed the pandemic had cut global life expectancy by 1.8 years to 71.4 years between 2019 and 2021, back to 2012 levels. By 2023, global life expectancy at birth had recovered to 73.3 years, against 73.4 years in 2019. Healthy life expectancy, which counts only years lived in full health, rose to 62.8 years but remained 0.4 years below its 2019 level, when COVID-19 first struck. The estimates, which track more than 160 diseases and injuries from 2000 to 2023, show “a global health landscape that is both recovering from the pandemic and continuing to evolve,” WHO said. “Living longer is one of the great achievements of public health,” said Dr Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Data, Digital Health, Analytics and AI. “The next challenge is to ensure that those additional years are lived in good health, while health systems are equipped to respond to the changing needs of populations.” Chronic diseases claim three in four lives; heart disease is still the top killer Eight of the 10 leading causes of death were noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), led by ischaemic heart disease, stroke and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). NCDs, which also include cancers, diabetes and dementia, accounted for 74% of deaths in 2023, up from 58% in 2000. For the first time, communicable diseases caused fewer than half of all deaths in low-income countries, which WHO called another step in the global epidemiological transition. Ischaemic heart disease killed about 9.5 million people in 2023, or 16% of the 61 million deaths worldwide, according to a WHO fact sheet published alongside the estimates. Deaths from the disease have risen by 3.0 million since 2000, the largest increase of any cause. Stroke killed 6.8 million people and COPD 3.6 million. Lower respiratory infections ranked fourth with 2.7 million deaths, back at their 2019 level and once again the deadliest communicable disease. Alzheimer disease and other dementias were the fifth leading cause of death, killing 2.1 million people. The conditions ranked 19th in 2000, and deaths have tripled since. Women accounted for 66% of dementia deaths. Deaths from HIV and AIDS fell 62% over the period, pushing the disease from seventh to 22nd. Diabetes, cancer and mental health conditions on the rise Diabetes deaths more than doubled to 2.0 million, while lung cancer deaths climbed from 1.1 million to 1.8 million. Kidney diseases rose from 17th to ninth, with deaths up 86%. Individual risk of ischaemic heart disease increased in WHO’s Western Pacific and South-East Asia regions even as the burden fell in much of the world. The risk of dying from diabetes also rose substantially, particularly in South-East Asia. The age-standardized rate of healthy life lost to depressive disorders rose by about 20% worldwide between 2019 and 2023, and by nearly 45% for anxiety disorders. WHO said mental health conditions and drug use disorders, alongside diabetes and dementia, were “contributing to a growing and changing burden of disease.” “The value of these estimates is not only in the numbers themselves,” Labrique said. “By showing how causes of death and disease burden are changing over time and across populations, they give countries evidence to help shape health policies and priorities.” Chronic diseases climb in low- and middle-income countries In low-income countries, seven of the 10 leading causes of death in 2023 were still communicable diseases. Lower respiratory infections have been the top killer there since around 2010, except in 2021, with more than 350,000 deaths every year since 2000 and no notable downward trend. Malaria, tuberculosis and HIV remained in the low-income top 10, though deaths from all three fell significantly. HIV deaths dropped 62%, and diarrhoeal disease deaths roughly halved, sliding from first to fifth. COPD, which ranks in the top 10 in every other income group, did not make the list. Lower-middle-income countries had a more even mix, with five NCDs, four communicable, maternal, neonatal or nutritional conditions and road injuries among their top 10. Deaths from ischaemic heart disease, stroke and COPD roughly doubled to take the top three places. Diabetes deaths more than tripled, lifting it from 15th to fifth, while HIV fell from sixth to 20th as deaths dropped about 70%. Upper-middle-income countries recorded the largest absolute rise in heart disease deaths of any group, nearly 1.8 million. Lung cancer deaths there more than doubled, an increase of 520,000 that is more than three times the combined rise in the other three income groups. It is also the only group where COVID-19 remained in the top 10, ranked 10th, though deaths have fallen 85% since the 2021 peak. Heart disease deaths fall in rich countries as dementia climbs High-income countries were the only group where deaths from ischaemic heart disease, stroke and stomach cancer fell, by 18%, 26% and 27% respectively. The two cardiovascular conditions still killed a combined 3.4 million people in 2023. Dementia deaths in high-income countries nearly quadrupled, lifting the conditions from seventh to third and past lung cancer. Hypertensive heart disease deaths more than doubled, rising from 15th to eighth. WHO attributed rising deaths from most leading causes in rich countries primarily to population ageing. “Understanding why people die is essential to improving how people live,” WHO said, while cautioning that accurate mortality data remain hard to collect in many low-income countries, where recording systems are often fragmented, incomplete or inconsistent. “When these data are disaggregated by factors such as age, sex and geographic location, they can reveal important inequalities and help identify where interventions are most urgently needed,” WHO said. title: Post-COVID Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction: A Focus on Persistent Diarrhea - Cureus

content_title: Post-COVID Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction: A Focus on Persistent Diarrhea
content: Abstract Persistent gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms after SARS-CoV-2 infection include diarrhea, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, constipation, nausea, and other disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs), but these entities should not be treated as interchangeable. In a meta-analysis of long-COVID studies, any GI symptom was reported in approximately 22% of patients and diarrhea in 10%, although heterogeneity was very high. In a large US Veterans Affairs cohort, post-acute COVID-19 was associated with incident diarrhea (hazard ratio {HR}: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.52-1.65; excess burden 7.99 per 1,000 persons at one year) and irritable bowel syndrome (HR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.28-1.86). Prospective Rome IV cohorts report lower absolute rates of formally diagnosed DGBIs; one study found persistent DGBI symptoms in 6.6% at six months, with functional diarrhea in 2.2% and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in 2.5% at three months. Mechanistic evidence supports intestinal involvement during acute infection and demonstrates associations with epithelial/angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) perturbation, immune activation, barrier dysfunction, altered microbial taxa, and impaired microbial metabolite production. However, persistent viral RNA or antigen, dysbiosis, and gut-lung signaling remain proposed or associative mechanisms rather than established causes of chronic diarrhea. Treatment evidence specific to post-COVID functional diarrhea is sparse. A large synbiotic trial improved a broad “gastrointestinal upset” domain in post-acute COVID syndrome, but did not enroll a defined chronic diarrhea or Rome-positive population; probiotic and fecal microbiota transplantation trials showing GI effects were largely conducted during acute COVID-19. Therefore, current care should first exclude organic and medication-related causes, then apply phenotype-based management extrapolated from established diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) and functional-diarrhea practice while clearly acknowledging the limited post-COVID-specific evidence. Standardized definitions, pre-infection GI data, appropriate controls, functional microbiome measures, and dedicated randomized trials are priorities for future research. Introduction & Background Post-acute gastrointestinal manifestations of SARS-CoV-2 infection span a broad spectrum. Patients may report persistent or new diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, altered appetite, dyspepsia, reflux, constipation, or other bowel symptoms after the acute infection [1-4]. These symptom reports are clinically important, but they are not synonymous with a functional bowel disorder or disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI). A DGBI is a positive clinical diagnosis based on a characteristic symptom pattern and accepted criteria after reasonable consideration of alternative organic disease; a symptom such as post-COVID diarrhea is initially a descriptive phenotype, not a diagnosis [5,6]. Acute GI involvement provides biologic plausibility for later bowel dysfunction. Diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, and anorexia were documented in early hospitalized and ambulatory cohorts, and viral RNA was detectable in stool in a substantial subset of patients [7-12]. Acute findings, however, should not be automatically extrapolated to chronic post-COVID symptoms because the relevant populations, time points, treatments, and competing causes differ. This review focuses on persistent or new-onset diarrhea after COVID-19 while placing it within the wider post-COVID GI spectrum. Diarrhea is emphasized because it is common enough to generate a measurable post-acute burden, overlaps clinically with functional diarrhea and diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D), and has direct implications for hydration, diagnostic evaluation, work capacity, and quality of life [1,3,4]. The review distinguishes broad post-COVID GI symptoms from Rome-defined DGBIs, separates acute from post-acute mechanistic and therapeutic evidence, and identifies where current management is based on post-COVID trials versus extrapolation from established gastroenterology practice. Review Methods of the narrative review This manuscript is a narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. For the peer-review revision, a targeted literature update was performed on September 19, 2026, using PubMed/MEDLINE for English-language publications from January 1, 2020, through September 19, 2026. The following two complementary search concepts were used: (1) (COVID-19 OR SARS-CoV-2) AND (long COVID OR post-COVID OR post-acute COVID-19 OR post-acute sequelae) AND (gastrointestinal OR diarrhea OR diarrhoea OR irritable bowel syndrome OR functional diarrhea OR disorders of gut-brain interaction OR microbiome OR dysbiosis); and (2) (COVID-19 OR SARS-CoV-2) AND (gastrointestinal OR diarrhea OR diarrhoea) AND (angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 {ACE2} OR permeability OR cytokine OR microbiome OR metabolite OR probiotic OR synbiotic OR fecal microbiota transplantation). We hand-checked reference lists of key systematic reviews, major cohort studies, randomized trials, and clinical guidelines for additional relevant publications. Eligible evidence included adult human observational studies, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews/meta-analyses, and major clinical guidance relevant to epidemiology, mechanisms, diagnosis, or treatment. Pediatric-only studies, animal-only studies, non-peer-reviewed preprints, isolated case reports, and studies without a relevant GI or post-infectious outcome were not prioritized. Acute-COVID studies were retained only when they directly informed GI mechanisms or intervention safety/efficacy and were explicitly identified as acute evidence. Duplicate publications were reconciled manually. Screening and synthesis were conducted at the narrative-review level; no independent dual-reviewer screening, formal risk-of-bias instrument, PRISMA flow diagram, or original quantitative pooling was performed. Effect estimates from the strongest studies are reported where available, and the limitations of this approach are addressed below. Terminology and scope For clarity, this review uses “post-COVID GI symptoms” as an umbrella description for GI complaints occurring after acute infection. “Post-COVID diarrhea” refers descriptively to persistent, recurrent, or new loose/watery stools after COVID-19 and does not imply a functional etiology. “Functional diarrhea” and “IBS-D” are Rome-defined DGBIs; IBS-D requires recurrent abdominal pain as a central feature, whereas functional diarrhea is characterized by loose/watery stools without predominant abdominal pain. “Post-infectious IBS” (PI-IBS) describes IBS that begins after an acute infectious illness in a person without pre-existing IBS. COVID-19 may act as an infectious trigger for PI-IBS, but a distinct “post-COVID IBS” mechanism has not been established [5,6,13,14]. Table 1 summarizes these operational distinctions among diarrhea-related post-COVID phenotypes. Epidemiology of post-COVID GI symptoms and DGBIs Quantitative Estimates The magnitude of post-COVID GI burden depends strongly on outcome definition. In a systematic review and meta-analysis of long COVID, the pooled frequency of any GI symptom was 22% (95% CI: 10%-41%); diarrhea was 10% (95% CI: 4%-23%), dyspepsia 20% (95% CI: 6%-50%), and IBS 17% (95% CI: 6%-37%). The very high heterogeneity (I2 approximately 96%-98% for several outcomes) limits use of these pooled percentages as patient-level predictions [3]. Large administrative cohorts quantify relative risk but may not establish a Rome-defined functional disorder. In the US Veterans Affairs study of 154,068 COVID-19 survivors, compared with contemporary controls, diarrhea had an HR of 1.58 (95% CI: 1.52-1.65) and an estimated excess one-year burden of 7.99 per 1,000 persons; IBS had an HR of 1.54 (95% CI: 1.28-1.86), and functional dyspepsia an HR of 1.36 (95% CI: 1.22-1.51) [1]. In a Bronx health-system cohort followed up to 3.5 years, 6.34% of 35,102 COVID-19 patients developed a new GI diagnosis versus 5.70% of controls; the adjusted HR for the composite GI outcome was 1.18 (95% CI: 1.12-1.25) [2]. These datasets demonstrate excess post-acute GI healthcare diagnoses but include outcomes broader than functional bowel disease. Prospective studies applying Rome IV criteria generally report lower absolute rates. Golla et al. followed 320 COVID-19 cases, 320 household controls, and 280 seronegative controls: 11.3% of cases reported new functional gastrointestinal disorder (FGID)/DGBI symptoms at one month, 8.4% at three months, and 6.6% at six months; at three months, IBS occurred in 2.5% and functional diarrhea in 2.2%, while no healthy controls developed FGID through six months [4]. In a separate case-control study, 5.3% of 280 COVID-19 patients met IBS criteria at six months, compared with one of 264 controls [15]. A 2024 meta-analysis estimated pooled post-COVID IBS incidence at 12%, but the pooled RR versus non-COVID controls was 1.23 (95% CI: 0.50-3.01), illustrating uncertainty generated by heterogeneous definitions, follow-up, and study design [16]. A 2025 multicenter analysis identified post-COVID DGBIs in 27 of 599 eligible patients (4.5%), again emphasizing that formally defined DGBIs represent a narrower group than all post-COVID GI symptoms [17]. Table 2 summarizes representative epidemiological studies and their quantitative findings. Diarrhea Versus Other GI Outcomes and Symptom Duration Diarrhea is a reproducible acute and post-acute symptom, but it is not uniformly the dominant late GI complaint. Acute meta-analyses primarily involving hospitalized patients estimated diarrhea around 7-8%, whereas long-COVID studies include dyspepsia, appetite disturbance, abdominal pain, constipation, and reflux-like symptoms at comparable or higher frequencies [3,8-11]. These estimates should not be combined across disease phases. A symptom present for several weeks after an infection may still represent resolving post-infectious illness; a Rome-defined DGBI requires a chronic, pattern-based diagnosis. Prospective studies showing decreasing symptom prevalence from one to six months support this distinction [4,15]. Demographic, Geographic, and Clinical Heterogeneity The most consistent prospective risk signal is the presence of GI symptoms during acute infection, with some cohorts also identifying greater acute disease severity and psychological comorbidity as predictors of later DGBI [4,15]. Evidence for a universal effect of sex, age, vaccination status, or variant is less consistent. Large database studies can adjust for measured comorbidities but incompletely capture diet, antibiotic exposure, access to care, health-seeking behavior, and pre-infection microbiome composition [1,2]. Variant and vaccination eras also overlap with changes in hospitalization practices and treatment, making causal attribution difficult. Accordingly, demographic or geographic differences should be interpreted as context-dependent rather than as a single reproducible risk profile. Pathophysiology and Mechanistic Evidence Figure 1 summarizes a plausible mechanistic framework while emphasizing that no single causal chain has been established. Many data supporting ACE2 perturbation, cytokine activation, permeability changes, and dysbiosis derive from acute infection or broad post-acute syndromes rather than patients with chronic diarrhea meeting Rome criteria [7,18-31]. Intestinal Infection, ACE2, and Viral Persistence The intestinal epithelium expresses ACE2 and entry-associated proteases, and experimental and clinical data support intestinal involvement during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection [7,20,23,27,29]. Altered ACE2-related signaling may affect amino-acid transport, antimicrobial peptide expression, epithelial integrity, and local immune regulation. These observations provide biologic plausibility but do not establish that ACE2 disruption persists as the cause of chronic diarrhea. Viral persistence requires careful terminology. In a longitudinal study of 113 people with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, fecal SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in 12.7% at four months and 3.8% at seven months, demonstrating prolonged RNA shedding but not necessarily replication-competent virus [21]. In an endoscopic study of 46 patients with inflammatory bowel disease approximately seven months after COVID-19, gut mucosal viral RNA was detected in 32 and nucleocapsid protein in 24; importantly, investigators were unable to culture virus from tissue [22]. This selected IBD cohort is not equivalent to a population with post-COVID functional diarrhea. Thus, RNA detection, antigen persistence, viable virus, and causal persistence-related diarrhea are distinct claims; only the first two have substantial human evidence in selected cohorts. Immune Activation and Mucosal Barrier Dysfunction Acute COVID-19 can produce cytokine and chemokine activation, epithelial injury, and markers compatible with increased intestinal permeability [7,18,26,27]. Barrier disruption can expose mucosal immune cells to microbial products and alter secretion or motility. However, direct evidence linking persistent cytokine activation or permeability abnormalities specifically to chronic post-COVID functional diarrhea is limited. Available post-acute studies often evaluate broad multisystem symptoms, small selected cohorts, or surrogate biomarkers rather than a well-phenotyped diarrhea endpoint. The most defensible interpretation is therefore that immune and barrier abnormalities are plausible contributors whose causal magnitude in chronic diarrhea remains uncertain. Microbiome, Microbial Taxa, and Metabolites Acute COVID-19 microbiome studies repeatedly report depletion of potentially beneficial commensals. In a two-hospital cohort, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, and bifidobacteria were underrepresented and remained reduced in serial samples collected up to 30 days after disease resolution [30]. In a prospective PACS cohort, patients with symptoms at six months had higher Ruminococcus gnavus and Bacteroides vulgatus and lower F. prausnitzii; butyrate-producing Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum and F. prausnitzii showed inverse correlations with PACS [28]. These PACS symptoms were predominantly non-GI, so the findings cannot be assumed to explain chronic diarrhea. Functional microbial changes may be as important as taxonomic shifts. In 66 antibiotic-naive COVID-19 patients, pathways for short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) and L-isoleucine biosynthesis were impaired and remained abnormal beyond 30 days after recovery; measured fecal SCFAs were also lower, with associations to severity and inflammatory markers [18]. GI-specific post-acute data are more limited but emerging; a study that followed 983 antibiotic-naive patients with mild COVID-19 identified distinct oral/gut microbial and serum metabolomic patterns in a small subset with GI symptoms at three months [31]. Bile-acid and tryptophan alterations have also been reported in acute/severe COVID-19 studies, but direct evidence connecting a specific bile-acid signature to persistent post-COVID functional diarrhea remains insufficient [25]. Confounding is a major limitation. Antibiotics, hospitalization, diet, geography, medications, acute disease severity, and baseline health can independently alter microbiome composition. Antibiotic-naive designs reduce one source of confounding, but most studies do not fully control diet, pre-infection microbiota, socioeconomic context, or all medication exposures [18,31]. Chronic diarrhea itself can alter microbial composition, creating reverse causation. Microbiome findings should therefore be interpreted as associations until longitudinal, pre-infection, functionally characterized studies demonstrate directionality. Gut-Brain and Proposed Gut-Lung Interactions The gut-brain axis integrates enteric neural, central nervous system, immune, endocrine, and microbial signaling. Post-infectious inflammation, stress, sleep disruption, altered diet, and changes in activity can interact with visceral sensitivity and motility without implying that symptoms are purely psychological [5,6,32]. This framework is well aligned with DGBI biology. By contrast, gut-lung communication is biologically plausible and relevant to systemic inflammation, but its specific role in chronic post-COVID diarrhea has not been established; it should be considered a proposed or incompletely defined pathway rather than a proven mechanism [25,26]. Figure 1 summarizes the proposed mechanisms linking SARS-CoV-2 infection with persistent gastrointestinal symptoms and disorders of gut-brain interaction. Table 3 summarizes the proposed mechanisms and the strength and limitations of current human evidence. Clinical Phenotypes and Relationship to PI-IBS Post-COVID bowel dysfunction may represent several different clinical pathways as follows: slow resolution of acute infectious diarrhea, an organic or medication-related disorder unmasked during/after infection, a new DGBI triggered by infection, or exacerbation of a pre-existing bowel disorder. The overlap with PI-IBS is substantial because both can follow infection and involve altered barrier function, low-grade immune activation, dysbiosis, visceral hypersensitivity, and gut-brain signaling [5,14,15,32]. Current evidence does not establish post-COVID bowel dysfunction as a single distinct disease entity. For a patient who develops classic IBS after COVID-19 and meets Rome criteria, COVID-19 is best conceptualized as a potential infectious trigger unless future biomarkers demonstrate a reproducibly distinct pathobiology. Duration is clinically important. Loose stools lasting days to a few weeks after acute illness can reflect transient recovery or treatment effects. content: Understanding 'Cicada COVID': Risks and Precautions This website uses cookies 🍪 We use cookies to ensure you get the best online experience. For more details, please see our Privacy and Cookie Policy. Read more. Accept Cookies Decline Cookies Home Special Medical Center Doctor Patient Services Packages About us Investor Relations Eng ไทย Eng 中文 1512 Doctor Schedule Find a Doctor Appointment Patient Services Hospital room Other Services News&Events Testimonials TV Programs Medical Publications Contracting Companies Insurance Partners Packages Health Check-up Package About us Vision and Mission Certificate CSR Activity Data Protection Policy Contact Us Job 1512 Language TH EN ZH Home Special Medical Center Doctor Schedule Find a Doctor Appointment Patient Services Hospital room Other Services News&Events Testimonials TV Programs Medical Publications Contracting Companies Insurance Partners Packages Health Check-up Package About us Vision and Mission Certificate CSR Activity Data Protection Policy Contact Us Job Investor Relations Home Media Article for health Understanding 'Cicada COVID': Risks and Precautions Understanding 'Cicada COVID': Risks and Precautions September 30 / 2026 Getting to know the new COVID variant “Cicada” (or BA.3.2), the latest sub-variant of Omicron that the World Health Organization (WHO) has designated as a “Variant Under Monitoring” (VUMs) due to numerous mutations in the spike protein, which may affect immune evasion. What is Cicada COVID... Does it come from insects? The name "Cicada" is just a nickname used for the BA.3.2 variant for easy international recognition. It is not related to insects and is not transmitted through insects in any way. Is it different or more severe than previous variants? Mutations: More than 50 genetic changes have been found, especially in the spike protein area, which helps the virus enter human cells and evade the immune system more effectively. Severity: From laboratory data, "there is no evidence yet that it causes increased severity" compared to other Omicron variants currently circulating. Its replication and transmission behavior remain at similar levels. Has it reached Thailand yet... Anything to worry about? Based on current surveillance and genomic sequencing, "no reports of the Cicada variant have been found in Thailand yet." It is mostly detected in small proportions (about 5-8%) in some countries such as South Africa, Australia, and the United States, so it is not the dominant variant globally at this time. How to prepare... Is there a vaccine yet? Currently, there is no vaccine specifically produced for the Cicada variant. However, having basic immunity still helps reduce the severity of the disease. The important thing is to take care of yourself according to familiar measures: Wash your hands frequently and avoid crowded places. Wear a mask when in high-risk areas or poorly ventilated spaces. Monitor for unusual symptoms such as fever, cough, or difficulty breathing. If symptoms occur, perform an ATK test and consult a doctor for an accurate diagnosis. content: Business&Talent Good News Barcelona Barcelona in figures Made in Barcelona Professionals Barcelona Global Young Talent Arts Events The Barcelonian The Bar of the Post Letters Music Scene Creativity Images Lifestyle Gastronomy Baco & Boca Hotels with history The Radar Unknown Faces Enjoy Barcelona From La Rambla to the world Interviews: A Granini with... Interviews: A 'ColaCao' with... Opinion Live Focus Espectacles BCN Close the sidebar Good News Barcelona The European Medicines Agency gives green light to Hipra vaccine The Catalan family business makes history in the medical and pharmaceutical sector by managing to commercialize the first COVID vaccine developed 100% in the European Union. Although the pandemic has subsided, its factory in Amer (Girona) is prepared to manufacture up to 600 million doses per year, which it will sell under the Bimervax brand at a price between 9.75 and 7 euros. Sergi Saborit 31 march of 2023 at 09:55h It has been a long time coming, but, finally, this Thursday Hipra has obtained the positive opinion from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) essential for the European Union to authorize the start of commercialization of its vaccine against covid-19, named Bimervax. According to the Catalan family company, in "a matter of hours" the European Commission will issue this authorization, which represents a historic milestone for the Catalan scientific and pharmaceutical sector and for Spain as a whole, as it is the first vaccine developed 100% in the European Union. Bimervax is also the first bivalent adjuvanted recombinant protein vaccine authorized in the EU against this virus, which gives it a differential character compared to the vaccines mostly used until now, based on messenger RNA technology. According to Hipra, it is a vaccine for people over 16 years of age especially indicated as a booster dose and that can help increase vaccination rates, as it causes fewer reactions and offers a "superior" duration of immunity compared to the vaccines previously on the market. "We have developed a vaccine that is very safe and, furthermore, it is less reactogenic than RNA vaccines, which represents a clear advantage for the population reluctant to vaccinate, tolerance is much better," assures Elia Torrella, executive vice president of Hipra and R&D director. According to the executive, Bimervax offers a very powerful "boost" as a fourth dose, provides protection against all existing variants of the virus and, furthermore, has the advantage that its logistics are very simple because it is "ready to use" ---it does not need to be reconstituted before use--- and because it does not require freezing: it must be stored refrigerated at a temperature between 2 and 8 degrees. "For Hipra, today is a very exciting and long-awaited day," said Torrella, who emphasizes that the new vaccine is the result "of the company's knowledge" and also of its "enthusiasm, perseverance and optimism" with the project. Unlike other pharmaceutical companies, Hipra has shown total transparency regarding the price of the new vaccine: each dose will cost between 9.75 euros and 7 euros, depending on the volume of purchase made by each State. And when can the first doses of Bimervax be injected? This is a decision that depends exclusively on the health authorities of the countries and the vaccination plans they activate, but Hipra assures that, in the best case, by the end of April they could deliver the vaccine to the warehouses that supply health centers. "We have enough stock of finished product and raw material to be able to supply all the vaccines they ask for during these first months," assures Carles Fàbrega, Hipra's human health director. According to the executive, the production capacity of the Amer (Girona) plant is 600 million doses per year, although this figure could be expanded to 1,000 million if necessary. Hipra has been manufacturing the Bimervax vaccine for months, which it can now start selling. The Girona-based company has already signed a pre-contract with 13 countries of the European Union that have the right ---though not the obligation--- to purchase up to 250 million doses. Of these 13 countries, a group of six ---including Spain--- had already communicated to the company their intention to make the first purchases once community authorization was obtained, so the first contracts could be formalized in the coming weeks. In parallel, Hipra is in negotiations with other non-EU countries, such as Malaysia and some states in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia, but everything was on stand by awaiting the EMA's decision. "Now we will begin the registration phase in the rest of the countries of the world and we will also request WHO authorization," explained Fàbrega. The company of the Nogareda family, which until now had focused solely on veterinary vaccines, has not wanted to reveal the amount of the investment it has made for the development of Bimervax, but assures that it is the "greatest economic and human effort" made to date. The bulk of the investment has been financed with its own resources, although Hipra has also received two public loans from the Center for Industrial Technological Development (CDTI) totaling 14.7 million euros, of which 10.82 million must be repaid. Economic impact due to approval delay The evaluation period for the vaccine by the European Medicines Agency has been longer than expected, as authorization has taken almost 12 months to arrive, compared to the express approvals of four months achieved by the first vaccines in the most acute phase of the pandemic. Hipra admits that this delay has had a negative economic impact because "it hinders market entry," in the sense that commercialization begins at a less opportune moment, as countries have high stocks of competitor vaccines and, furthermore, there is a widespread perception that the pandemic has already passed, which has led to a drastic drop in revaccination rates. Elia Torrella and Carles Fàbrega during this Thursday's press conference. "Covid-19 is here to stay; there is a general scientific consensus that it will be necessary to continue vaccinating, especially certain population groups. It is very important to have more vaccines to keep covid under control, so there is clearly space in the market for a vaccine like Bimervax, we are very happy to have finally received approval," Torrella highlighted. Along the same lines, Fàbrega defends that the new Catalan vaccine "fits perfectly with the needs of the global population," although he declined to make sales forecasts for this first year. Hipra also highlights another factor that states should consider when deciding whether or not to acquire their vaccine: "it is not good to vaccinate exclusively with a single technology", referring to the fact that currently the vaccines supplied are RNA and not recombinant protein. According to Torrella, the system they have used "facilitates the body's immune response" by introducing into the body a protein previously designed in a laboratory that generates antibodies, instead of the cells performing this step. Furthermore, it is a bivalent vaccine, which means that instead of one, it contains two proteins to fight against two different variants, in this case Beta and Alpha of SARS-CoV-2. "It is a much more versatile vaccine, because it is a two-in-one", Torrella pointed out, after noting that if new variants appeared, the vaccine could be adapted in just four months. Bimervax technology is widely used and known in vaccine manufacturing, such as for hepatitis and influenza. Hipra carries out the entire production process in Amer, which allows it to gain response capacity. The board has thanked the entire team of Hipra professionals for the enormous effort made and, especially, all the volunteers who participated in the clinical trials that were necessary to obtain the EMA's approval. According to Hipra, the EMA's positive opinion comes after concluding that "it has sufficient solid data on the quality, immunogenicity and safety of the vaccine." "In phase IIb and III studies, it has been shown that it is a safe, low-reactogenic vaccine with a broad capacity to neutralize the main variants of SARS-CoV-2, including the Omicron variants. In the comparative study versus the mRNA vaccine required by the EMA, it is shown that, 6 months after receiving the booster dose, people vaccinated with the Hipra vaccine present higher levels of neutralizing antibodies against all the variants studied, which suggests more lasting protection. In the same comparative study, it is shown to have less reactogenicity than the RNA vaccine," they add. Filed in Good News Barcelona User Consent Prompt Focus Prompt

content: ABC News Live Video Local News Shows Good Morning America ShopGMA Interest Successfully Added We'll notify you here with news about Turn on desktop notifications for breaking stories about interest? OffOn Stream on WHO says suspected hantavirus cluster 'is not the start of a COVID pandemic' There are 12 suspected cases so far. ByMary Kekatos and Zoe Magee May 7, 2026, 4:39 PM Share Follow ABC News on Google An epidemiologist from the World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday that the suspected hantavirus cluster aboard a cruise ship is not the beginning of another COVID-19 pandemic. Eight cases are currently being reported by the WHO, including five laboratory-confirmed cases and three suspected cases. Of those eight cases, three have died. Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, an infectious disease epidemiologist and acting director of epidemic and pandemic management at the WHO, was asked during a press conference what the difference was between this cluster and the early days of the COVID pandemic. Related Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US "I want to be unequivocal here. This is not SARS-CoV-2. This is not the start of a COVID pandemic. This is an outbreak that we see on a ship," Van Kerkhove said. Van Kerkhove explained that hantavirus doesn't spread in the same way that coronaviruses do, but rather through "close, intimate contact." Most hantaviruses don't transmit from person to person. "The actions that are being taken on board [the ship] are precautionary to prevent any onward spread," she added. Health personnel assisting patients onto a boat from the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images There appears to be two confirmed cases and four suspected cases that have not been added to the WHO's official count yet. The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport confirmed that two patients infected with the virus are currently hospitalized in the Netherlands, one at Radboud University Medical Center and the other at Leiden University Medical Center. Additionally, two Singapore residents who were on board the ship are currently being monitored. Singapore's Communicable Diseases Agency said it was notified of the individuals on May 4 and 5. "They have been isolated at the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, where they are being tested for hantavirus. The risk to the general public in Singapore is currently low," the agency said. The agency added that test results are pending, with one resident having a runny nose. The other is asymptomatic. The French Health Ministry also issued a statement on Thursday that a French national has been tested after they displayed mild symptoms. This person had been in contact with one of the confirmed cases. Related 3 people waiting to be medically evacuated from cruise ship at center of suspected hantavirus outbreak Three deaths have been recorded so far, including a married Dutch couple. The 70-year-old male patient died on April 11, and his body was taken off the ship on the island of St. Helena on April 24. His 69-year-old wife disembarked on the same day, and her health rapidly deteriorated. She died at a South Africa hospital on April 26. A third passenger, a German woman, presented with pneumonia symptoms starting on April 28, according to the WHO. The woman died on May 2 from causes not yet known, according to Oceanwide Expeditions, which operates the cruise ship. The WHO said 29 people disembarked on St. Helena on the same day that the body of the Dutch male patient and his wife disembarked. They traveled to 12 countries: Canada, Switzerland, Germany, Denmark, Great Britain, St. Kitts and Nevis, Netherlands, New Zealand, Singapore, Sweden, Turkey and the United States. Popular Reads Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys 2 days ago Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials 13 hours ago District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Sep 29 The disembarked guests have all been contacted by Oceanwide Expeditions. In the U.S., local authorities in five states -- Arizona, California, Georgia, Texas and Virginia -- are monitoring the disembarked passengers and are conducting contact tracing, None have shown signs of illness at this time. Anais Legend, technical lead for viral hemorrhagic fevers at WHO, said during the press conference on Thursday that "step-by-step guidance is being developed" for the disembarked passengers and that the WHO is coordinating with national authorities. Anyone with any signs of symptoms will be isolated while other passengers have their risk exposure evaluated. The cruise ship MV Hondius, carrying passengers suspected of having cases of hantavirus on board, leaves Praia, Cape Verde, May 6, 2026. Reuters Public health experts said they expected a more robust response from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Institutes of Health. "CDC would typically be asked by WHO to, or by a country to, help in technical assistance," Dr. Carlos del Rio, an H. Cliff Sauls distinguished professor of medicine at the Emory University School of Medicine, told reporters on Thursday. Typically, CDC teams would be deployed to an area, he said, and the teams would perform contact tracing and interviews and conduct an outbreak investigation. "I would envision by now, many, many days ago, we would have seen ... a team from CDC deployed to the area," he added. Related 3 dead in suspected hantavirus outbreak aboard a cruise ship: What to know Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the IDSA, added that she would have expected a CDC press briefing, an alert from the agency's Health Alert Network or information from the NIH on potential treatments in the pipeline that could receive emergency use authorization to help treat hantavirus patients. Marrazzo said she is not aware that conversations about potential therapies at NIH aren't happening but it "does not give me a lot of assurance or reassurance that we're not hearing about any of it." The CDC posted a statement on X on Wednesday on behalf of NIH Director and acting CDC director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya that read, "Our hearts go out to the passengers aboard the cruise ship M/V Hondius and their families during this difficult time. Our CDC team began coordinating with domestic and international partners as soon as we were notified of a hantavirus situation." The statement said there is "clear, written health guidance to the American passengers through the State Department" and that the CDC "will continue to update as more information becomes available and remains committed to protecting the health and safety of the American public." The agency also published a statement on its website stating that the Trump administration "is closely monitoring the situation" and that the Department of State "is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." The CDC also said the risk to the American public is "extremely low." The WHO said during Thursday's press briefing that the U.S. is coordinating with the global health agency in a technical capacity. Because the cluster is limited and confined to a cruise ship, the "idea of sending messages across the world and panicking everyone is not required," said Dr. Abdirahman Mahmoud, director of the WHO's health emergency alert and response operations. He added that the WHO is "informally" aware that contact tracing has been done of the U.S. passengers who disembarked last month and are back home. title: New ‘atlas’ of respiratory infections suggests Covid is no longer just a winter virus - EL PAÍS English

content_title: New ‘atlas’ of respiratory infections suggests Covid is no longer just a winter virus
content: Oriol Güell Barcelona - OCT 02, 2026 - 04:40 EDT Share on Whatsapp Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Prefer EL PAÍS on Google Compartir: Whatsapp Facebook Twitter Bluesky Linkedin Copy link A comprehensive atlas of the 18 main respiratory viruses circulating in Catalonia, produced for the first time in Spain by researchers from that northeastern region, reveals that the coronavirus that caused the Covid-16 pandemic — SARS-CoV-2 — “is currently not a winter virus. In recent years, it has shown clear peaks during the spring and summer, which is different from what was initially expected.” This behavior has caused a clear mismatch with the current vaccination calendar . “We are immunizing at-risk groups [older people, those with chronic illnesses...] in the autumn, when the virus’ epidemic waves have already passed, and not beforehand, as would be desirable. This work raises the possibility that it may be necessary to adjust the planning of vaccination campaigns and guidelines,” warns Jacobo Mendioroz, deputy director general for Surveillance and Public Health of the Catalan government. The research’s findings, based on Catalonia’s healthcare system data between 2022 and 2025, have been observed this year again in the real world. Coronavirus incidence surged at the end of summer, when communities had not yet begun the vaccination campaign against this pathogen, which is administered alongside the flu shot. The new research highlights SARS-CoV-2’s behavior, more erratic after the pandemic but now showing mainly “a clear summer epidemic pattern .” Juan Carlos Galán, head of Virology at Ramón y Cajal Hospital in Madrid, considers the research highly relevant but says it is still too early to classify the coronavirus as exclusively a summer virus: “There are recent data from other European countries, and some areas of Spain, that point more to a biennial incidence, in summer and winter. What was observed in Catalonia over these three seasons indicates a trend in SARS-CoV-2 behavior, but we do not know whether other viral or environmental factors could have impacted that finding and we will have to wait for the next seasons to confirm it.” This expert highlights the study’s contribution to a “fascinating field” he calls viral ecology. “We see that there are interferences and, at times, what appears to be competition among different viruses. A good example was the first year of the pandemic, when influenza disappeared completely, overwhelmed by covid. This apparent antagonism between flu and SARS-CoV-2 is observed in subsequent years. Each virus unfolds on the calendar in an orderly way, as if occupying different niches. Many factors intervene in this process, even if they are not fully understood,” he concludes. Changing vaccination campaigns For Gregorio Montes Salas, secretary general of the Spanish Society of Preventive Medicine, Public Health and Healthcare Management (SEMPSPGS), the study confirms that “the coronavirus has not followed the expected winter pattern, at least so far.” He adds that this raises the option of “considering the possibility of de-seasonalizing vaccination against SARS-CoV-2.” Mendioroz and Montes Salas agree that before making decisions “it will be necessary to wait for further research,” given the logistical complexity of changing campaigns and the risk of undermining achieved coverage (65% for flu among those 65 and older and 50% for coronavirus). The underlying idea is that, even if belated, it is preferable for at-risk people to be immunized by taking advantage of the momentum of regional autumn campaigns rather than spreading doses across the year and losing adherence. “Campaigns make mass vaccination easier. Changing dates requires a logistical effort that must be carefully studied, but it may be something worth exploring,” Montes Salas says. “The whole organization, the messaging and even public perception would change. The risk is that coverage could drop: who is going to get vaccinated at the start of summer against a virus that has always been associated with cold weather?” adds Mendioroz. The paper was published in the latest issue of Eurosurveillance — the scientific journal of the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) — and its main aim was to obtain a detailed picture of respiratory virus circulation. “Influenza has always been monitored and, more recently, Covid and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). But what about the others? The answer provides key information: it helps plan prevention measures, prepare health centers or hospitals for peaks in demand and even anticipate what might happen,” Mendioroz says. One reason this is possible, the study’s conclusions argue, is that “respiratory viruses mainly follow a predictable pattern, appearing one after another in a consistent order every year.” “We know, for example, that the flu wave is successively preceded by a rhinovirus wave and then a parainfluenza wave,” the Generalitat’s deputy director general for Surveillance illustrates. The researchers analyzed more than 33,000 samples obtained between October 2022 and September 2025 by the Information System for Infection Surveillance in Catalonia (SIVIC), the sentinel network that monitors respiratory viruses in real time. The panel tracks the following viruses and subtypes: three influenza A strains and one B, two RSV strains, SARS-CoV-2, two seasonal coronaviruses (NL63 and OC43), four parainfluenza types, and one each of the following groups: rhinovirus, enterovirus, adenovirus, metapneumovirus and bocavirus. Influenza A shows the clearest seasonal pattern, according to the paper. Its peak usually occurs in Spain between late December and early February, although most often it happens in the second half of January. “Meanwhile, influenza B displays a less regular seasonality” and is usually offset from that peak, the researchers conclude. RSV also has a clear winter pattern, although in this case it precedes the flu by a few weeks and typically “reaches its peak roughly a month before it.” Rhinoviruses and enteroviruses, which cause mild cold-like illnesses, instead show a two-wave pattern, with peaks in autumn (September–October) and spring. Rhinovirus circulation also “declines when SARS-CoV-2 is circulating strongly,” the paper notes. Another group of pathogens that infect the respiratory tract maintains a very different profile and shows a constant presence “throughout the year, without clearly defined epidemic peaks.” This is the case for adenoviruses, some coronaviruses other than SARS-CoV-2 (such as NL63) and two parainfluenza types (1 and 4). The study also details the sequence of the remaining pathogens: parainfluenza virus 2 slightly precedes influenza, while metapneumovirus — a pathogen very common in childhood — and parainfluenza 3 emerge just as influenza begins to decline. Meanwhile, bocavirus and the seasonal coronavirus OC43 begin activity in mid-autumn, but their incidence rises slowly to reach peaks between February and April. Uthmeier alleges Pfizer misled Florida about its COVID vaccine’s safety

by Michael Moline, Florida Phoenix
October 1, 2026

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit Thursday against Pfizer Inc., alleging unfair and deceptive marketing of Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine.

The suit, filed in state trial court in St. Lucie County, also names Albert Bourla, the company’s chairman and CEO.

It seeks monetary damages for each violation of Florida law plus an injunction against future violations.

“Pfizer’s conduct misled Florida consumers when they were making some of the most sensitive health decisions of their lives. Ultimately, Pfizer’s misconduct rests on the paternalistic assumption that Florida consumers could not be trusted with the truth about Pfizer’s products. That offensive assumption is anathema to the principles underlying the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (‘FDUTPA’),” it asserts.

Uthmeier denounced the company in a video posted on X.

In response, Pfizer issued a written statement.

“We are proud to have developed the COVID-19 vaccine in record time in the midst of a global pandemic and saved countless lives. The representations made by Pfizer about its COVID-19 vaccine have been accurate and science-based, and the Company stands behind the safety and efficacy of its vaccine. Pfizer believes that the state’s allegations have no merit and will respond to the suit in due course.”

“Pfizer is deeply committed to the well-being of the patients it serves. Since its initial authorization by FDA in December 2020, the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine has been administered to billions of people, demonstrated a favorable safety profile in all age groups, and helped protect against severe COVID-19 outcomes, including hospitalization and death.”

Florida’s complaint recalls the scary time when Americans confronted a new virus that filled hospitals and impelled government leaders to close nonessential businesses, including in Florida initially.

Gov. Ron DeSantis later changed course, easing business restrictions and surrounding himself with COVID skeptics including Joseph Ladapo, whom the governor installed as Florida surgeon general.

“Florida citizens faced an unprecedented level of uncertainty” and “worried about how to protect their loved ones and themselves from a previously unknown virus” and resulting “once-in-a-generation economic shock,” the complaint reads. The company “bet big” its mRNA vaccine, it adds.

To overcome skepticism over the novel vaccine, the company undertook an intensive marketing campaign attesting to the vaccine’s safety, the document continues.

“Pfizer was not content merely to promote its own narrative. It also sought to quash any dissent that might impact consumer demand — like calling those who dared to question Pfizer’s public claims ‘criminals.’”

At the same time, the complaint says, Pfizer’s “record-breaking profits rested on deception and falsehoods. While Pfizer was insisting to consumers that the vaccine posed no material safety risks — and while it actively sought to discredit those who said otherwise — Pfizer was aware of data reflecting serious safety risks that it hid from the public.”

In January 2025, a Florida statewide grand jury found no evidence that COVID-19 vaccine manufacturers broke federal or state laws when making and distributing the shots. That was more than two years after DeSantis asked the Florida Supreme Court to assemble it to investigate alleged wrongdoing related to the COVID-19 vaccines.

The report did criticize what it considered too-close relationships between regulatory agencies such as the Food and Drug Administration and Pfizer and Moderna.

content: tyla homepage tyla homepage News Politics Entertainment Celebrity Entertainment Celebrity Life Animals Food & Drink Women's Health Mental Health Sex & Relationships Travel Real Life TV & Film True Crime Tyla Recommends Astrology Beauty Hair Make-up Skincare Style Home Categories Home>Life Published 14:42 30 Sep 2026 GMT+1 Difference between Covid and flu symptoms as cases surge across UK The UKHSA has issued fresh data on the seasonal rise of Covid-19 and the flu Madison Burgess Follow us on Google Discover The September sickness has officially arrived - and people are being taken down left, right, and centre by sniffling noses, endless coughing, headaches, and high temperatures. If you’ve been forced to call in sick to work in the past few weeks, you wouldn’t be the only one, as the latest UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) data has highlighted a surge in both the flu and Covid-19 this month. As reported by The Mirror, in the week of 24 September, hospital admissions with Covid increased from 0.81 per 100,000 people to 1.2 per 100,000 people, which is an almost 50 per cent rise. However, the UKHSA has reassured that this is actually an expected level for this time of year. Advert Meanwhile, Influenza cases also increased, and the illness is currently circulating at baseline levels. Advert Emergency department attendances for influenza-like-illnessincreased also last week and were above seasonally expected levels. Seasonal illnesses are ramping up again in the UK (Getty Stock Image) As outlined by Manchester Evening News, out of those tested via a GP swab, 10.7% tested positive for flu, which is up from 8.3% the previous week. With both of these seasonal illnesses on the rise, it can be difficult to tell which one you’re actually dealing with, especially since some of the symptoms overlap. Advert The biggest difference is that a sudden loss of taste or smell is common for Covid-19, but very rare with the flu. And as per Mayo Clinic, seasonal flu symptoms usually show up quickly, about one to four days after you're around someone who is sick. Covid-19 symptoms, on the other hand, generally appear two to 14 days later. However, there are also a lot of similarities, such as fever, a dry cough, shortness of breath or trouble breathing, feeling tired, a sore throat, a headache, a runny or stuffy nose, and muscle aches. The flu and Covid-19 have a lot of similar symptoms (Getty Stock Image) Symptoms of Covid-19 As per the NHS, the most common symptoms of Covid-19 are: A high temperature – you may feel hot, cold or shivery, or your skin is hot to touch on your chest or back (you do not need to measure your temperature) A new, continuous cough – this means coughing a lot for more than an hour, or 3 or more coughing episodes in 24 hours A loss or change to your sense of smell or taste Shortness of breath Feeling tired or exhausted An aching body A headache A sore throat A blocked or runny nose Loss of appetite Diarrhoea Feeling sick or being sick The NHS advises that if you think you have Covid-19, you should try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people if you or your child have symptoms and either: Have a high temperature Do not feel well enough to go to work, school, childcare, or do your normal activities You can go back to your normal activities when you feel better or do not have a high temperature, and if your child has mild symptoms such as a runny nose, sore throat, or mild cough, and they feel well enough, they can go to school or childcare. Advert Last week, hospital admissions with Covid increased from 0.81 per 100,000 people to 1.2 per 100,000 people (Getty Stock Image) Symptoms of flu Flu symptoms come on very quickly and can include: A sudden high temperature An aching body Feeling tired or exhausted A dry cough A sore throat A headache Difficulty sleeping Loss of appetite The symptoms are similar for children, but they can also have ear pain, sore eyes, swollen glands, and appear less active. Advert You can find more information about both Covid-19 and the flu on the NHS website.
